title: Coroner recommends hospital fix cross-border communication after death
text:
A coroner is calling for health departments in New South Wales and Victoria to coordinate a streamlined electronic record system for Albury Wodonga Health (AWH) following the death of a 46-year-old woman.

Deputy State Coroner Rebecca Hosking made the recommendation as part of her findings into the death of Kate Manley, who died in the early hours of November 16, 2022 at Albury Hospital.

The inquest focused on whether Ms Manley received adequate care and appropriate treatment during her admission to the acute mental health unit Nolan House and the hospital's medical wards between November 11 and 16, 2022.

Kate Manley was remembered as someone who was independent, strong, beautiful and full of energy. (Supplied: Manley family)

Nolan House is based in NSW, but is also subject to Victorian laws.

Under a memorandum of understanding between the Victorian and NSW Health Departments, AWH must comply with laws in both states regarding the provision of mental health services.

During earlier inquest hearings, AWH executive Danielle McLeish said the hospital had several combined systems in place to track patient movements and comply with the laws of both states, but managing them was at times confusing for staff.

Ms Hosking found that, on the night of her death, Ms Manley had waited nearly five hours to be transferred from the mental health unit to a medical ward.

"Given the level of deterioration, her transfer ought to have been undertaken more quickly," Ms Hosking said.

It was found that Ms Manley would have benefited from immediate intravenous (IV) therapy.

However, Ms Hosking found there was no evidence that a quicker transfer could have prevented Ms Manley's death.

No food or fluids for two days

Ms Manley had a history of schizophrenia, depression and other medical issues, with multiple admissions to Nolan House from 2006 to 2017.

On November 9, she saw her doctor for mental health concerns.

Two days later, her partner took her to Albury Hospital after her mental health declined.

Kate Manley was transferred to Nolan House. (Supplied: Albury Wodonga Health)

Upon assessment, she was moved to Nolan House, diagnosed with catatonia, and had little interaction with staff.

The inquest heard she was resistant to some medical tests and also upset about being moved to the acute mental ward.

Her fluid and food intake was poor during her stay there and at one stage, she went nearly 48 hours without eating or drinking.

On November 15, as her condition worsened, staff planned to transfer her to a medical ward for closer monitoring, when the transfer delay occurred.

Just after midnight, she stopped breathing, and CPR was performed.

It was later determined that Ms Manley had died from a pulmonary embolism, a sudden blood clot in a lung artery.

No VTE assessment undertaken

Ms Hosking found venous thromboembolism (VTE) assessments during Ms Manley's stay at Nolan House were inappropriate and clearer protocols were needed to distinguish psychiatric from physical treatment.

Vishal Bhargava, the first doctor to see Ms Manley, said a VTE risk assessment was warranted, but he was not concerned because she was moving around.

AWH policy requires VTE risk assessment within 24 hours of admission.

"She was not given prophylaxis and her VTE risk increased as her mobility and hydration decreased," Ms Hosking said.

"The intertwining of physical and psychological symptoms was such that Nolan House could not provide Kate with the holistic treatment she required."

Ms Hosking also said at the time of Ms Manley's death, standards and policies were not well known because some medical practitioners missed orientation or because locum and agency staff were used.

It was also found Nolan House psychiatrists knew catatonia increased VTE risk but hesitated to prescribe Clexane, believing it was the medical team's role.

Kate Manley died of a pulmonary embolism at Albury Hospital in the early hours of November 16, 2022. (ABC News: Annie Brown)

In her findings, Ms Hosking recommended health departments in NSW and Victoria consider implementing a treatment pathway for catatonia patients and audit VTE risk assessments.

It was noted that Albury Wodonga Health said it had updated VTE risk policies and staff orientation after Ms Manley's death.

The inquest heard a new hospital communications tool was also being introduced to improve staff coordination.

In her findings, Ms Hosking suggested Ms Manley's death could be used as a case study when training hospital staff in shared physical and mental health care.

Remembered as having a heart of gold

During the inquest, a family statement described Ms Manley as a treasured family member, with her daughter, Ruby, being the "centre of her world".

"[Kate] was compassionate, creative and had drive … [and] brought fun, warmth and laughter into the lives of those who knew her," the family statement said.

Rachel Anderson remembers her friend Kate Manley (right) as a fun and creative woman. (ABC News: Philippe Perez)

Ms Manley's friend Rachel Anderson also attended hearings and remembered her as a fun and creative woman.

"She was one of my best friends [and] we did a lot together," Ms Anderson said.

" She was like a bright light … always did things spontaneously [and] she had a heart of gold. "

Ms Anderson said if policies at the hospital had been followed, Ms Manley could have been with her today.

Rachel Anderson believes that if proper procedures had been followed, her best friend may still be alive. (ABC News: Philippe Perez)

"I just feel like there needs to be some accountability on behalf of Albury Wodonga Health and I feel that Kate needs justice," she said.

"As a result, she's now gone forever, which hurts deeply."

title: Uncertainty over job loss numbers as TMAG faces staff cut
text:
The state government has maintained Hobart's Tasmanian Museum and Art Gallery (TMAG) is not cutting its workforce by 30 per cent, despite claims by the public sector union and the opposition.

The Community and Public Sector Union (CPSU) said an online meeting was held last week, where staff were told that 19.7 full-time-equivalent jobs (FTE) would be cut by the end of the financial year.

It is not clear whether the job cuts would be made through redundancies or natural attrition, or which roles could be affected.

TMAG houses permanent exhibitions on the thylacine, Antarctica, Palawa history and culture, and Tasmanian plant and animal specimens. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden )

However, a government spokesperson has said the claim of nearly 20 FTE jobs was false, and that "TMAG is not required to reduce its workforce by 30 per cent".

Tasmania's Deputy Premier Guy Barnett also denounced the claims as false, but said that "across government there need to be efficiencies".

The exact size of TMAG's workforce is not publicly available, but the ABC understands it to be between 50 and 75 people.

TMAG states it is Australia's second-oldest museum. It houses permanent exhibitions on the thylacine, Antarctica, Palawa history and culture, and Tasmanian plant and animal specimens.

TMAG holds and displays important Tasmanian cultural items, including pelts and taxidermy of the extinct thylacine. (TMAG)

In addition to the main museum building in the Hobart city centre, TMAG also has a collections and research facility at Rosny.

More than 280,000 visitors walked through TMAG's doors in 2024—25, of which half of them were from interstate and nearly a fifth from overseas.

No clear number on job loss

In question time on Tuesday, Labor MP Meg Brown asked about the CPSU's claim.

"Minister, staff are saying one thing, and your government is saying another. What is actually going on at TMAG and exactly how many jobs will be cut at the end of this year?" she said.

TMAG also has a research and collection facility in Rosny, on Hobart's eastern shore. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

In his answer, Arts Minister Roger Jaensch noted there were job cuts across the department overseeing TMAG, including at the gallery.

The former Department of State Growth is being reformed as Building Tasmania, and will slim its focus to infrastructure.

As part of this move, 250 jobs will be lost.

"This does not automatically translate to an automatic cut of 19 TMAG positions," Mr Jaensch said.

He did not say how many jobs would be cut at TMAG.

A government spokesperson also could not confirm how many jobs had been cut from Building Tasmania as part of the changes.

Staff cuts to have 'profound effect'

In a letter to members last week, the union said "staff have a right to be angry" about the decision.

"There is simply no way to soften the impact of what is being proposed," the letter reads. "These cuts will have a profound effect on staff, on the services TMAG delivers and on the preservation of Tasmania's cultural and scientific heritage."

Loading...

The union said the cuts were "impossible to reconcile" with "a government that repeatedly promotes tourism as a key economic driver".

CPSU state secretary Thirza White said the government needed to be clear about where the jobs were coming from and what the resulting potential service reductions would be.

"We know already that in the past six months there have been days when they haven't had enough staff to adequately open all of the galleries," she said.

Government subsidies to several creative TasTAFE courses have ended. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Government cutting 250 jobs from former department

The job cuts at TMAG come as the state government makes sweeping cuts to Tasmania's public service workforce in an attempt to get the budget under control.

Clarion call for 'highly vulnerable' underfunded Tasmanian arts "Dangerously low" arts sector funding has rendered the Tasmanian industry "highly vulnerable", with funding stagnant since 2016-17, the state government has conceded.

Treasurer Eric Abetz is eyeing 1,800 job cuts by 2032 to help curb state debt, which topped $6 billion this year.

As part of the changes to Building Tasmania, TMAG will be overseen by a yet-to-be-established Tourism, Events and Creative entity within the Department of Premier and Cabinet.

The latest job losses follow concerns the Rockliff government was underfunding creative sectors.

This year, the state government cut several TAFE courses, including in apparel, fashion and textiles; screen and media; graphic design; and music.

Subsidies for those courses were cut last October.

Last year, a briefing to former arts minister Madeline Ogilvie warned that "dangerously low" funding levels had rendered the industry "highly vulnerable".

The state government announced a $10 million creative industries fund in this year's state budget, with the money flowing to Screen Tasmania and Arts Tasmania.

However, Screen Tasmania, the state agency responsible for funding and developing TV, film and games, has recently cut its number of staff from five to two.

title: Energy watchdog slaps down billion-dollar bailout for transmission line
text:
Australia's biggest transmission company has been slapped down by the regulator over attempts to pass on a billion-dollar bill to consumers for a bungled high-voltage power line.

The Australian Energy Regulator (AER) this morning rejected Transgrid's bid to recover a huge cost blowout on its part of Project Energy Connect, a $3.6 billion transmission line linking South Australia with New South Wales.

In a "preliminary position" published today, the watchdog said it was not satisfied with Transgrid's claims the blowout was unforeseeable, and failure to finish the project would imperil the grid.

The decision is a blow for Transgrid, which now faces the prospect of being unable to claw back much of the extra money it has had to spend to finish Project Energy Connect.

Consumer advocates have cheered the regulator's announcement, saying it sets an important precedent.

Craig Memery from the Justice and Equity Centre said the AER, in denying Transgrid, was drawing a line between legitimate claims and superficial ones.

'Extension cord to nowhere' The high-voltage powerline project linking SA to NSW is running dramatically over time and budget.

In doing so, Mr Memery said the regulator was looking after consumers, who would have to pay for any approved extra spending through their bills for decades.

"At the end of the day, it is about whether companies pay for their mistakes," Mr Memery said.

"It's also about who carries what risk.

" We would argue that some of what has happened here is Transgrid has erroneously misjudged risk. "

Events 'not unforeseeable'

Today's announcement by the AER comes after a six-month review of Transgrid's claims for the bailout.

Under Australia's energy laws, transmission companies are subject to regulation which guarantees their revenues — and the prices they can charge — under five-year deals.

But after trouble with Project Energy Connect, Transgrid wanted to reopen its deal that was locked in for the period between 2023 and 2028.

When the spending plan was first approved by the regulator, the project was expected to cost about $2.3 billion.

Of this, Transgrid's share amounted to almost $1.9 billion, with its South Australian counterpart ElectraNet given $457 million.

ElectraNet finished its part of the project in December 2023, on time and on budget.

Transgrid's share, however, is now estimated to cost more than $3 billion.

AER dismissed Transgrid's claims that the security of the national electricity system would be jeopardised. (ABC News: Kenith Png)

According to Transgrid, it could not have foreseen the failure of its contract with Clough and Spanish engineering giant Elecnor.

Transgrid said the project had been hit with a series of setbacks that were outside its control, from flooding to COVID-19 and extreme inflation.

It warned that unless Project Energy Connect was completed in good time, the security of the national electricity system would be jeopardised.

However, the regulator dismissed those claims.

The AER questioned whether the events leading up to the contract failure were truly outside Transgrid's control.

And it rebuffed suggestions the grid would be at risk without Project Energy Connect.

"Transgrid has not demonstrated that failing to deliver, or materially delaying, PEC would be likely to materially adversely affect the reliability or security of the relevant transmission system," the regulator noted in its reasons.

An energy 'litmus test'

Mr Memery said for too long Australia's energy regulations had seemed to serve poles-and-wires companies first and consumers second.

He said the AER had now shown that it was not a soft touch.

What is more, he said it was about time, given the pipeline of high-voltage power line projects that were under construction or in the planning stages.

Rewiring the planet Countries across the globe are racing to rewire their electricity systems for a decarbonised future. In Australia, delays are mounting, along with doubts about whether it can meet goals on schedule.

Taken together, Mr Memery said the projects were worth tens of billions of dollars, and the transmission companies needed to be held accountable for their spending.

"This is a bit of a litmus test really for the whole regulatory regime," Mr Memery said.

"If the AER were to approve this request by Transgrid, it would open the door for a lot of claims that shift risk from businesses to people.

"It'll shift that risk from the businesses that are regulated to the people who are meant to be served by that regulation.

"And so, the AER's response really does start to put that back onto Transgrid, the business, to manage their own risks.

" They're responsible for the inability to foresee events that could have been foreseen. "

Construction work on the Energy Connect transmission line. (Supplied: Elecnor Australia)

While the AER provisionally dismissed Transgrid's "reopener" claims, the regulator said the company could still apply to recover extra spending in its next revenue deal from 2028.

A spokesman for Transgrid said the company respected the independence of the regulator and would "carefully consider" its comments.

But the spokesman stressed today's announcement was not the final say by the AER on the matter and it did not "determine whether prudent and efficient project costs" may ultimately be recovered.

"Energy Connect is a nation-critical project that is already strengthening interconnection between states and will provide long-term benefits for consumers through improved energy sharing, increased access to renewable generation and lower wholesale electricity costs," the spokesman said.

"The paper recognises the substantial benefits the project is expected to deliver."

title: $150k payment for part-time work not a 'significant' sum, says Perrottet
text:
The brother of former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet has defended a $150,000 yearly payment made to his wife for an average of 16 hours a week of work, describing it as not a "significant" amount.

The payment was made by Beckington, a company linked to lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood, who was working with fugitive property developer Jean Nassif and his company Toplace.

The NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) inquiry has previously heard that Anita Perrottet worked an average of 16 hours a week through her company, Macquarie Consulting, for Mr Greenwood's businesses and received more than $660,000 over about two-and-a-half years.

On Tuesday, counsel assisting the commission Peggy Dwyer SC asked Ms Perrottet's husband Charles Perrottet, a key member of the inquiry, whether he agreed $150,000 was a significant figure for work done on a "flexible level".

"$150,000 for a year's worth of work, I don't think, is a significant amount of money," Mr Perrottet said.

"Value is in the eye of the beholder. If there were value, if Jeremy had seen value in the work, he was paying accordingly."

Anita Perrottet gave evidence last week. (ABC News)

Mr Perrottet also told the public hearing that some of the money paid to Macquarie Consulting also covered advice he personally provided to Mr Greenwood about Toplace.

The evidence differs from an account given by Ms Perrottet last week, when she told the commission the payments were for her own consulting work and that neither she nor her husband had worked to benefit Toplace.

Dr Dwyer challenged Mr Perrottet over why he did not disclose the arrangement in earlier private hearings and whether he told his wife some of the money was compensation for his advice.

Dwyer: "Did you deliberately hide it from your wife?" Perrottet: "I wouldn't say deliberately hide it, but I wanted her … that she felt valued. She was doing a lot of good work for Jeremy." Dwyer: "Sure, but did you just want to patronise Anita so that she thought she was genuinely charging for this work when, in fact, it was your advice?" Perrottet: "No, not at all. She was doing a lot of good work. She had her own, relationship with Jeremy. She had a negotiation with Jeremy on how much you would be paid. The invoices reflected, the advice I gave and hers. I just don't can't tell you how much I disclosed to Anita."

The key figures in ICAC investigation Eight weeks of public hearings by the ICAC that could change the NSW Liberal Party forever begin on Monday.

ICAC is examining whether payments made through companies linked to Mr Greenwood were genuine consulting fees or used to disguise money intended for political purposes.

It is investigating allegations that prohibited political donations were channelled through third parties to support the NSW Liberal Party's right-wing faction and advance Mr Nassif's interests.

Dominic Perrottet is not accused of wrongdoing.

title: Cats coach speaks for first time since club's concussion fine
text:
Geelong coach Chris Scott insists he is unsure if Jake Kolodjashnij will play for the Cats again following the club's concussion saga.

Speaking for the first time since Geelong was fined $140,000 for failing to officially let the AFL know about the concussion waiver in Kolodjashnij's contract, Scott kept it brief.

The dual premiership coach referred back to the club's response and was adamant he had stayed out of dealings about Kolodjashnij's future.

Geelong fined over concussion scandal The AFL hands down its penalty after a meeting between the commission and Geelong regarding Jake Kolodjashnij's now-controversial contract.

Kolodjashnij, who came forward as the player involved shortly after the story broke and has not played at any level since, returned to the club last week ahead of the finals.

If the defender does play it will almost certainly be at VFL level, with the club premiership favourites to win the second-tier competition.

"I've been really conscious to separate myself from this," Scott said about Kolodjashnij.

"This is one of those situations [where] if I could help, I would.

"But I'm told, and I believe independently, that I just wouldn't be any assistance, so I just don't get in the way."

The penalty was $100,000, plus a suspended sanction of $40,000, which stems from the league fining Geelong last October after an investigation into the club's third-party agreements.

"Hand on heart, I don't really even know the facts, so I'm certainly not going to be swayed by people who understand the facts less than I do," Scott said.

"So my go-to is that I just support the club's position … whether some people accept that wholeheartedly, that's something you can ask them privately.

"But the club's position is, it's best for us to say, 'OK we acknowledge certain aspects, and we're keen to move forward.'"

After having the pre-finals bye, Geelong will face red-hot Carlton in an elimination final at the MCG on Friday night.

Speaking on Monday, experienced midfielder Tom Atkins denied the saga was a distraction for the Cats as they aimed to win their fifth premiership this century.

AAP

title: Phones and computers are about to be more expensive — thanks to AI
text:
Smartphone prices are on the rise, and the reasons come down to the business of AI.

Beneath the surface, smartphones contain thousands of individual parts.

The internal workings of smartphones rely heavily on memory.

Lurking behind the screen, the battery, the speakers and the camera, a single chip is the main thing keeping your phone running.

Memory chips are crucial to all modern smartphones, as well as much of our other everyday technology.

This is the dynamic random-access memory chip (DRAM), the short-term working memory inside your phone.

It's what lets you switch quickly between apps while your phone processes information.

DRAM chips are at the centre of escalating tech costs. ( )

And if you're looking to buy a new phone, this chip could be the reason it's about to cost you a whole lot more.

The rise of AI data centres is making memory chips a scarce commodity and consumers are paying the price.

The memory problem does not stop with your phone.

Those same DRAM and NAND chips also live inside your laptop, desktop computers and gaming consoles.

And right now, there are not enough of them to go around.

Last year, NAND and RAM memory were both incredibly cheap. At one point, a 16-gigabyte RAM chip cost as little as $4.76.

But that began skyrocketing in late 2025 and that same chip could cost you almost $60 as of June, according to the WA Data Science Innovation Hub (WADSIH).

The budget smartphone market is the latest victim of the global shortage, with multiple tech bosses saying memory chips are now their most expensive component.

Samsung has already hiked the price of its phones and its tablet line-up, making devices with higher storage up to $115 more expensive.

Microsoft, Google and Apple have also raised the price of several different phones, computers and tablets over the past few months.

In February, video game developer Valve announced it was pushing back the launch of its newest hardware due to uncertainty about memory.

Then in June, it revealed its Steam Machine would cost $US1,049 ($1,511), hundreds of dollars more than the pre-shortage price estimated by several industry outlets.

Smart TVs, digital cameras and smart home devices could be the next to face price hikes.

Data centres eat the chips business

There's also a third type of memory involved in the market: high-bandwidth memory, or HBM.

This is the specialised, high-speed type of memory used to power artificial intelligence (AI) servers.

Inside an AI data centre, HBM allows an AI system to process large amounts of data very quickly, training it even faster.

A data centre can require tens of thousands of memory chips. ( )

This HBM chip was made by SK Hynix. ( )

But AI systems need a lot of HBM chips to keep running and memory manufacturers are trying to keep up with skyrocketing demand.

Alex Jenkins is the director of the WA Data Science Innovation Hub and says the memory supply chain has been deliberately redirected.

"There's only three companies in the world that really make DRAM, they control over 90 per cent of the market," Mr Jenkins says, referencing Micron, SK Hynix and Samsung, who also make high-bandwidth memory.

As well as needing a different kind of memory, AI also burns through it at a much faster rate, requiring thousands of servers to train and keep running.

"When we train an AI, we don't use one AI server. We might use 10,000 AI servers," Mr Jenkins says.

" Services like ChatGPT, in order to train that AI, we're looking at entire data centres, 200,000 AI chips all working together. "

The sheer amount of chips needed, Mr Jenkins adds, makes it much more profitable for manufacturers to shift to producing HBM RAM for AI companies.

"Essentially all these memory manufacturers decided, 'Well, why am I even bothering making DRAM, which I'm selling at near cost price, when I can make HBM RAM, and make a very healthy margin and make lots of money that way'."

Priced out of digital worlds

Laura Alice Bracken is a Geelong-based artist and creative technologist, who uses programming and software in her work.

Sometimes that means transforming energy generated by moss into an interactive animation.

Other times, she's creating a "cyberdeck" — a custom-built, portable computer — set into a vintage decorative seashell.

Laura Alice Bracken is a Geelong-based artist and creative technologist. ( )

Laura Alice Bracken's new media artworks use creative coding techniques and rely heavily on modern technologies. ( )

Rising tech prices are making immersive art like this piece from Laura Alice Bracken difficult to afford. ( )

Access to the internet means people can teach themselves tech and animation, but the memory shortage is changing things in a way that's "frustrating", she says.

"About two years ago, I was thinking about upgrading my GPU [graphics processing unit]. I was starting to get bigger renders, bigger jobs and I wanted to have something that could push it.

"I started to save for it, and then … I just started watching the prices go up and up and up and up.

"And I was like, 'Oh no, I've missed the boat.' And now [that upgrade] is just so far outside of my price range, there's just no way."

And it's not just hobbyists who are feeling the pinch.

Independent researchers and smaller AI companies are also facing shortages, according to Shuai Wang, a research fellow at the University of Queensland's ielab.

"More and more in the computer science field, when we go to conferences, we see that companies [are starting] to make more and more impact," Dr Wang says.

"Ten years ago, it was the research institutes making the impact.

"But it's not because the research institutes are becoming less smart, it's because they don't have enough resources."

Bracken says the soaring prices mean new artists may be priced out of the field. And others are shifting to less high-tech artwork and design, something she thinks is connected to price hikes.

"People are starting to realise that these price rises are not necessarily going anywhere [and] they're starting to futureproof their understanding of tech," she says.

Years of price hikes forecast

Some industry think tanks have predicted the memory crunch could last about two years, until more fabrication plants or "fabs" come online.

SK Hynix's chairman, Chey Tae-won, took a more dire view, predicting in March the shortage could persist into 2030.

"HBM requires a large number of wafers … it is physically impossible to suddenly increase wafers in the short term," he told reporters in California.

"Securing more wafers takes at least four to five years."

In the meantime, phones and other technology will not only cost more — cheaper, entry-level electronics could go off the market entirely.

Memory is now the most expensive component of a smartphone. ( )

Low-end products are already "becoming unprofitable", global technology research firm Omdia stated in recent analysis.

Many companies, according to Omdia, have returned to cheaper, older screens and cameras to accommodate the price of RAM.

And at least one company, gaming console brand Ayaneo, suspended pre-orders for an upcoming release, citing rising memory costs.

And there's no incentive for memory manufacturers to change, according to Dr Wang.

"It becomes a competition," he says.

"All of [the AI companies] want to acquire and reserve those resources, and they actually tend to buy more at higher and higher prices."

It will be at least another two years of shortages and price hikes before more capacity comes online, Mr Jenkins says.

"It's enormously complex and it takes a long time," he says.

Credits

title: New hope in quest to solve mystery of MND hotspots
text:
Professor Dominic Rowe has cared for countless patients with motor neurone disease (MND) and in 2013 established Macquarie University's MND Research Centre.

But there are still things about the as-yet-incurable neurological condition that remain a mystery even to experts.

Professor Rowe said MND cases had increased by 300 per cent across Australia in the past 37 years, with rural areas hit the hardest.

"Our recent mortality paper shows that if you live in rural and regional Australia, you are 40 per cent more likely to die from motor neurone disease. This cannot be genetic," he said.

"If they don't have a genetic cause, what's happened occupationally, recreationally, or even where they live to cause their motor neurone disease?"

Notifiable condition

Finding an answer to those questions might be about to get easier.

From today, any NSW doctor making an MND diagnosis will have to report the patient's age, address, occupation, date of onset and other demographic and clinical information to NSW Health.

Professor Rowe said the decision to make MND a notifiable condition could provide crucial extra data for researchers to analyse.

"We can now intensely study these patients to work out what's going on in their environment to cause it," he said.

Regional hot spots

Much attention will be focused on MND hotspots which include regional centres such as Griffith, Leeton, Wagga Wagga and Narrandera in the Riverina where rates of the degenerative illness are estimated to be five to seven times the national average.

Other areas of concern include Tamworth, Coffs Harbour and Port Macquarie.

Previous research has suggested a link between cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) blooms in waterways and MND.

But Professor Rowe said more work was needed before any conclusions could be drawn.

"There are also lots of other agents that are released into these water systems that may cause the algal bloom in the first place. So it is quite a complex thing," he said.

Lake Wyangan in Griffith has been identified as an MND hotspot. (ABC Riverina: Nicola Ceccato)

Griffith resident Tania Magochi was diagnosed with MND in 2011.

She has a family history of the disease, but also grew up near Lake Wyangan, which is prone to outbreaks of blue-green algae.

"As kids we used to go out there [to the lake] all the time, like every weekend, and we used to ride down the little slide into the pool all the time," she said.

"Since the scientists said there was a connection, I avoid it at all costs … I won't even let my children go there."

Ms Magochi said she hoped making MND a notifiable disease in NSW would help provide some answers.

"Not just me, but for our scientists to understand where all these people are coming from so they can understand the environmental factors around that area," she said.

"The only hope that we have is that we can find a treatment.

" At the moment we're sent home with nothing, so just to have a possible treatment would mean the world to all of us with MND. "

Lake Wyangan is prone to blue-green algae blooms, as captured in 2020. (ABC News: Ben Deacon)

Philip Orr from the Australian Rivers Institute at Griffith University has been studying blue-green algae for close to four decades and has monitored Lake Wyangan's water quality over that time.

He said as areas like Griffith were heavily agricultural, looking into what caused the blooms in the first place would be beneficial.

"Saxotoxin [the neurotoxin produced by the algae in the lake] … you either die or you don't, and there's no chronic long-term effects from it," Dr Orr said.

"To die you'd have to drink the scum … there's no definitive research that shows [it causes] MND."

Phillip Orr has studied Lake Wyangan's water for more than three decades. (Supplied)

Dr Orr recently worked with Griffith City Council, which has tried a variety of methods to control algae in the lake, including chemical trials, water isolation and recirculating water.

"From my study of the water quality in Lake Wyangan, the water quality is not as bad as the public might like to think it is," he said.

Blue-green algae warning signs are around Lake Wyangan near Griffith. (ABC News: Rachel Carbonell)

"I think council are doing the right thing; they've really got the future of the lake well and truly in their sights in terms of how to manage it.

"But whatever they do, it's going to be a long-term solution."

title: Sharks want to play their home NRL finals match at their home ground
text:
Cameron McInnes would not be surprised to see the NRL deny Cronulla a home final at Shark Park, warning players were now used to head office making rule changes "at the drop of a hat".

Out of form on the eve of finals, the fifth-placed Sharks are nevertheless guaranteed to host a week-one elimination match against one of South Sydney, North Queensland or Newcastle.

But the finals suitability of dilapidated Shark Park, the NRL's lowest-capacity regular venue at 15,000 seats, has been a discussion point in recent years.

ABC NRL Daily podcast Andrew Moore and the ABC NRL team bring you your daily dose of NRL conversation. The team give you the context and depth beyond the headlines.

The NRL pockets ticket sales from finals games so would take a financial hit from hosting in the shire rather than the Sydney Football Stadium or Stadium Australia, which each have more than twice the capacity.

Shark Park has been deemed unfit for use in week two or three of the finals, but hosted week-one finals matches in 2022, 2023 and 2025.

The NRL is unlikely to publicly confirm venues until after round 27 finishes this Sunday, and told clubs in the pre-season it had the discretion to determine where finals games were played.

The possibility of playing elsewhere did not sit well with England-bound McInnes, who could be playing his last game at Shark Park against Melbourne this Saturday.

"I was under the impression the rule was if you earn a home semi, whether you're first or second, or fifth or sixth, you get to play it at your home. Our home is Shark Park," he said.

"I don't know if that was a rule change that they can just put in, but then again, the NRL changes rules all the time.

"Rule changes just happen at the drop of a hat now, don't they? So as a player, you just have to adapt."

The league most recently trialled a change to the kick-off rule in Melbourne's defeat of Brisbane last week, having introduced six-agains, 20/40 kicks, two-point field goals and captain's challenges since the start of the decade.

The NRL has also made less prominent changes to its trainer and interchange policies in that time, as well as reverting to one on-field referee per game.

"How much do you need to change? I understand at the end of the day, it's entertainment, I get it," McInnes said.

"But it's like someone's constantly sitting there going, 'The game's going really well, but now let's change something else'."

Inconsistency around ruck infringements was most dismaying to veteran McInnes, who sympathised with the league's match officials.

"When you bring that [six-again rule] in, I get it, to speed the game up and have the speeds to score long-range tries with fatigue, but it also creates an inconsistency in the game," he said.

"[It's] hard for the refs, isn't it? Because it's so subjective.

"If someone gets hit in the face and is offside, that's clear as day, but with the six-agains, it's just sort of a lottery."

title: Former rival says Nick Kyrgios's drug ban 'pretty much expected'
text:
Stefanos Tsitsipas says he was not surprised when Nick Kyrgios was suspended from tennis for drug use.

Kyrgios was banned earlier this month after he revealed he tested positive for cocaine in June when he was in Spain to play at an event.

The Australian could be suspended for four years, though a lighter punishment is expected.

Tsitsipas was asked about Kyrgios on Monday after upsetting 10th-seeded Arthur Fils in the first round of the US Open.

The former world number three, who had a famously contentious relationship with Kyrgios, said he was surprised the suspension did not come sooner.

"I mean, to be entirely honest with you, I knew about this before the announcement. Myself, I knew about it," Tsitsipas said.

"So, what can I tell you? I will just tell you the truth. I knew about all of this before any announcement was made, and when I saw it on social media, I was, like, 'Here we go'. I kind of expected it, to be honest."

Tsitsipas and Kyrgios played a fiery match at Wimbledon in 2022 , when Kyrgios reached his only Grand Slam final. Tsitsipas blasted a couple of shots directly at Kyrgios, intentionally hit a ball into the crowd, and afterward called Kyrgios a "bully".

Kyrgios has largely battled injuries since and said when he was suspended that he had felt "helpless and alone", though added that "none of that excuses what I did".

Nor did it come as a shock to Tsitsipas.

"I knew that those were things that were happening away from the tennis courts. I will tell you that," he said.

"I'm not going to try and cover up someone that I know the truth for. I'll consider myself a nice person with everyone, but these were behaviours that I personally heard on the tour and heard other people in that same environment saying those sort of things to me.

"So, when I saw it, I was like, 'Well, pretty much expected, to be honest'. I am surprised it came so late, though."

title: 'Canberrans suing their own government' costing ACT tens of millions
text:
Legal action taken against the ACT government continues to cost the territory tens of millions of dollars each year, with the price of medical negligence payouts on the rise.

Newly released answers to questions taken on notice during budget estimates reveal the ACT Insurance Authority (ACTIA) paid out $60.7 million in damages, settlements and legal costs relating to medical negligence claims last financial year.

In 2024-25, the territory paid more than $39 million for the same medical negligence-related costs, and in 2023-24 that figure was about $28.6 million.

Independent MLA Thomas Emerson said it was concerning that medical negligence payouts had more than doubled over a two-year period.

"Certainly, some lawsuits will not be avoidable, and we can understand as a community that our government will be exposed to some extent to liability claims," he said.

"But seeing a more than doubling of medical negligence, damages and settlements over just a two-year period is seriously concerning — both from a medical perspective, and also from a budgetary perspective.

"How many health procedures could have been provided by investing sufficiently in the health system to avoid the medical negligence claims that have been put forward?"

Thomas Emerson says the ACT government should review the impact of increasing legal bills on the territory's finances. (ABC News: Dave Sciasci)

Footpath-related injury payouts

ACTIA also paid out nearly $2.8 million on footpath-related personal injury claims last financial year.

In 2024-25, the amount paid out for footpath-related injury claims was about $1.72 million, and in 2023-24 it was just more than $1 million.

In 2025-26, the government spent nearly $7.2 million on footpath maintenance and repairs, meaning the cost of paying out personal injury claims was 38 per cent of what the government spent on footpath maintenance.

Footpath-related personal injury claims cost the ACT government more than $2.7 million in the last financial year. (Supplied: Stuart Poole)

"This is evidence that the government is not investing upstream and actually addressing the issues that are leading to harm in our community," Mr Emerson said.

"Because of that, we as taxpayers are having to pay more downstream in legal costs and payouts because of the government having not fulfilled its duties."

Mr Emerson also noted that $3.2 million was spent settling eight of the 85 institutional abuse claims opened in the past three financial years, suggesting there may be a bill of over $30 million for the outstanding cases.

'Cost of incompetence'

Mr Emerson said the cost of "Canberrans suing their own government" was having a big budgetary impact.

"These figures show the whole-of-government cost of incompetence is massive. They're pretty shocking figures," he said.

"While not every lawsuit is avoidable, the ACT government should be closely investigating the impact of its growing legal bill on the territory's finances."

The ACT government paid out more than $60 millions in damages, settlements, and legal costs for medical negligence claims in the last financial year. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

Mr Emerson said his criticism was not directed toward "Canberrans pursuing their own legal rights, but instead of the escalation in claims and damages that we're seeing".

"The scale of legal costs and payouts revealed through these questions presents a huge opportunity for the ACT government to pursue budgetary savings and reduce community harm," he said.

"It's such a cop-out for the government to complain about assembly committees criticising their fiscal performance while Canberrans are literally suing them for their failures."

'Really crude numbers'

But Health Minister Marisa Paterson said the figures did not provide the full picture, and that the government had been settling more cases in a timelier manner.

"These are really crude numbers, so they don't provide any explanation of what is actually happening," she said.

"I think the government is getting better at settling these type of matters in a timely way and managing historical matters as well.

"And also there have been a couple of large settlements too."

Marisa Paterson says the government has been settling more cases. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

She said the government had learned from the cases and was always looking to make improvements.

"Particularly in the medical negligence space, in terms of many of these issues have been inquiries and there have been recommendations," she said.

"Obviously when … anything like this happens, the government does look into what has been the cause, and it's about continuous improvement to ensure these things don't happen again."

title: Messi's legendary run for Argentina almost never happened after heartbreak
text:
Lionel Messi's retirement from the Argentina national side brings down the curtain on one of world football's most storied international careers.

The records and achievements of Messi are stuff of legend, and his status in international sport is reserved for only the very greatest of their craft.

Messi was denied the perfect finish to his Argentina career in July, defeated in a thrilling FIFA World Cup final by Spain that went to extra time.

But the loss in New Jersey only denied the fairytale finish, and did not diminish the legend that Messi created for himself, or the legacy that he has left among his people.

But the love and admiration of his people, the two Copa America wins, and the 2022 FIFA World Cup triumph, which brought Argentina back to the pinnacle of world football and raised Messi to the legendary status of fellow countryman Diego Maradona, almost never happened.

Legend at Barca, struggles with Argentina

Messi has been on top of world football for two decades, winning the coveted Ballon d'Or as the world's best player a staggering eight times.

From 2004 to 2021, he won 10 La Liga titles, seven Spanish Cups, seven Spanish Super Cups, four Champions Leagues, three UEFA Super Cups and three FIFA Club World Cups with Barcelona.

Football great Lionel Messi announces retirement from Argentina team The announcement comes just weeks after the death of his father Jorge.

In a legendary 2012, he scored 91 goals in all competitions, a record haul for a calendar year, and slotted 50 goals in the 2011-12 La Liga season.

Trophies, accolades, love and admiration grew and grew for the Barcelona great, but success for Argentina was not forthcoming.

Coming through the ranks, Messi led Argentina to a Youth World Championship in 2005 and the Olympic medal at the Beijing Games in 2008.

But in the very big tournaments, trophies were harder to come by.

When Messi made his senior debut for Argentina in 2005 against Hungary, the South American giants had not won a trophy since the 1993 Copa America.

Messi's final tears As the champion wept on the pitch after the World Cup final defeat, Argentina may well have wondered with trepidation what life will look like in the post-Messi era.

Messi's Argentina senior debut was nothing to write home about either, sent off after less than a minute on the pitch for elbowing an opponent.

But Messi overcame that infamous beginning to establish himself as a star, and the hope of a nation that Argentina could return to the top of South America, and the world.

What followed was a string of bitter disappointments.

Argentina made the final of the Copa America in 2007, but was soundly beaten 3-0 by arch rival Brazil.

At the 2010 FIFA World Cup in South Africa, Messi failed to score at the tournament as Argentina exited at the quarterfinal stage.

Argentina was then knocked out again at the quarterfinal stage, this time at the 2011 Copa America, by eventual winner Uruguay.

These were bitter disappointments for Argentina and Messi, but the pain was about to increase, and it led to the great man announcing he did not want to be part of it anymore.

Three years, three finals, three painful defeats

Heading into the 2014 FIFA World Cup in Brazil, it had been 21 years since Argentina's last major trophy.

But the blue and whites marched into enemy territory intending to claim international football's greatest prize, and doing it in the backyard of their greatest rival.

Loading...

Argentina won all three group games — over Bosnia and Herzegovina, Iran, and Nigeria — to top the group, beat Switzerland 1-0 in extra time, and finally won a quarterfinal by defeating Belgium 1-0.

A scoreless semifinal against the Netherlands, finalists in 2010, went to penalties, where Argentina won 4-2, including a successful spot kick from Messi.

But the joy ended there.

In a major final for the first time in seven years, Argentina faced a German side that had just humiliated Brazil 7-1 in the semifinal.

Like all of Argentina's games to that point, the game was tight and tense. It went to extra time, but the strike of German Mario Götze sealed Germany's triumph.

A photograph of Messi looking at the World Cup trophy after the defeat, captured by Bao Tailiang for Chengdu Economic Daily in China, became the defining image of Messi for years.

Lionel Messi walking past the FIFA World Cup trophy after defeat in the 2014 final. (Supplied: Bao Tailiang for Chengdu Economic Daily via X)

The heartbreak only continued for Messi and Argentina.

The Copa America was held in 2015 and 2016, with Argentina reaching the final both times and losing to Chile each time.

Both finals ended scoreless and went to penalties. Messi converted his penalty, the only Argentinian player to do so, in the 2015 defeat, but the great man missed his spot kick in 2016.

The pain of the 2016 final defeat was too much for Messi, who announced he was retiring from Argentina.

"For me, the national team is over," he said after the loss to Chile in 2016. "I've done all I can. It hurts not to be a champion."

"It's been four finals, I tried.

"It was the thing I wanted the most, but I couldn't get it, so I think it's over.

"I think this is best for everyone. First of all for me, then for everyone.

"I think there's a lot of people who want this, who obviously are not satisfied, as we are not satisfied reaching a final and not winning it."

World football was that close to never seeing Messi reach the heights he would achieve.

Six-week retirement, 10 years of legacy building

When Messi announced on Sunday, June 26, 2016, that he would no longer play for Argentina, he ended what was by any other measure a magnificent international career.

He had made 113 appearances, scored 55 goals and led his country to four major finals.

But the absence of a trophy was not good enough — not for someone as great as Messi.

On July 10, the world watched Cristiano Ronaldo lift an international major trophy as Portugal won the 2016 Euros.

On August 12, Messi announced that he was back.

What followed after his six-week retirement is, on its own, one of the greatest international careers ever forged.

Messi would add another 94 caps to his name, score another 70 goals, and more importantly, end Argentina's trophy drought.

And Messi didn't just win one major trophy for Argentina; he won four.

The 2018 FIFA World Cup in Russia was another familiar quarterfinal exit for Argentina, but it was the precursor to an era of success.

Argentina finally broke through to win the Copa America in 2021, and they did it against Brazil, in Brazil.

Lionel Messi was thrown into the air in celebatrion after Argentina ended a 28-year trophy drought. (Getty Images: MB Media)

With the COVID-19 pandemic keeping many fans away from the famed Maracanã Stadium in Rio, Argentina ground out a 1-0 win to claim the nation's first major trophy in 28 years.

Messi was hoisted in the air by teammates in images that went around the world.

The drought was over, and the rain was here to stay. Argentina won a second trophy in 2022 when they defeated European champions Italy in the relaunched Finalissima, but greater prizes were to come.

By this stage, Messi had surpassed everything achieved by Maradona, except one.

Maradona almost single-handedly won the World Cup for Argentina in 1986, and gave him a legendary status that was near God-like.

Now, it was Messi's time to do the same.

He did it in Qatar at the 2022 World Cup, leading the blue and whites back to the top of world football.

The final against France, the defending world champions, was anything but ordinary. Those who were accustomed to Argentina grinding out 1-0 wins got the shock of their lives when they traded blows with France in one of the greatest finals ever played.

Messi scored two goals, including in extra time, while Ángel Di María also scored for Argentina. But the South Americans met their match in France, or more specifically, Kylian Mbappé, who scored a hat-trick, including a 118th-minute penalty to send the final to spot kicks.

In the penalty shootout, Messi converted, Mbappé converted.

Argentina was perfect. France was not.

When Gonzalo Montiel's shot hit the back of the net, Argentina was world champion and Messi had reached the God-like status that had only been reserved for Maradona.

The image of Messi kissing the World Cup became the defining image of his illustrious career.

Lionel Messi finally got his hands on the FIFA World Cup trophy, which had eluded him for so long. (Getty Images: China News Service/VCG/Cui Nan)

One more trophy would follow for Argentina, another Copa America in 2024 to make it three major trophies in four years.

That trophy was icing on the cake for Messi's legacy, which by now was in uncharted territory.

Messi's international career by numbers

1

Lionel Messi led Argentina to the FIFA World Cup title in 2022. He also led his country to two more finals, 2014 and 2026, which both resulted in 1-0 defeats in extra time.

2

Lionel Messi led Argentina to two Copa America titles in 2021 and 2024. Before then, the last time Argentina was champion in the Copa America was in 1993.

6

Lionel Messi has played in a record six FIFA World Cups — 2006, 2010, 2014, 2018, 2022 and 2026. Only Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo has also managed that feat.

21

Lionel Messi scored 21 goals at the FIFA World Cup finals. He is second on the all-time list behind French star Kylian Mbappé, who has scored 22 from just three tournaments.

34

Lionel Messi holds the record for the most FIFA World Cup finals matches played. He was on the field 34 times for Argentina in a FIFA World Cup tournament. Ronaldo is second on the list with 27 appearances for Portugal.

125

Lionel Messi holds the Argentina goal-scoring record, netting 125 times for his country. That is more than double the previous record holder, Gabriel Batistuta, who scored 54 times for his country.

207

Lionel Messi made 207 appearances for Argentina, a national record. He made his debut in 2005 against Hungary, and played his final match against Spain in the 2026 FIFA World Cup final. Ronaldo holds the world record for international appearances, playing 233 times for Portugal.

title: Labuschagne dropped as Australia names ODI squad for African series
text:
Australia has named its ODI squad for its back-to-back series in Zimbabwe and South Africa later this month, with World Cup winner Marnus Labuschagne among five players dropped.

Australia are reigning ODI world champions, after a stunning final win over India in Ahmedabad in 2023.

Labuschagne scored a half-century in that final, but his struggles since then have led to him being dropped from the ODI squad that will play in Africa, almost a year out from the next World Cup, which will be held in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia.

Labuschagne has missed five of Australia's previous 56 ODIs, but the 32-year-old has been dropped, along with Matt Short, Ben Dwarshuis, Todd Murphy and Liam Scott, from the squad picked to play in Pakistan and Bangladesh in May and June.

Pat Cummins and Mitch Starc will play in the ODIs against South Africa, while Mitch Marsh and Travis Head return after not playing in Pakistan or Bangladesh.

Emerging stars Cooper Connolly, Oliver Peake and Joel Davies have been added to the Australian ODI squad.

SBS has secured the rights to broadcast the FIFA World Cup 2030 in a $30 million-plus bid to remain “the spiritual home of football” after this year’s blockbuster event. The public broadcaster’s boss Jane Palfreyman said she was thrilled to see the tournament stay on SBS after more than 18 million fans watched the recent World Cup on the network over June and July. SBS chief executive Jane Palfreyman has claimed the rights to the World Cup for the broadcaster. Ben Symons Palfreyman declined to comment on the price SBS has agreed to pay, though sources with knowledge of the deal said it is above the $30 million rumoured to have been paid for the 2026 tournament. She said the World Cup was an opportunity to celebrate Australia’s modern culture. “We saw with this World Cup, it really brings Australians together across cultures, languages, and communities. We know that most Australians support not just one team, but two or three, so it’s the Socceroos plus a second or third team, either based on their sporting prowess or cultural heritage,” Palfreyman said ahead of SBS’ annual content showcase to media buyers in Sydney on Tuesday.

Advertisement

The costs of sports rights continue to rise, even as advertising revenues flowing to free-to-air television broadcasters have fallen drastically over the past five years. Live sports and news are the two remaining categories guaranteed to deliver audiences to TV networks, as evidenced by this year’s Cup which was held across Canada, Mexico and the United States – more than 1 million Australians watched 64 of its 104 matches. This year’s edition was held in a favourable time zone for Australians, with the majority of matches kicking off during daylight hours, and the latter stage games at 5am. But the next edition will be jointly hosted by Spain, Portugal and Morocco, which are eight hours behind Australia’s Eastern Standard Time in winter. There will also be one match held in each of Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay to mark the centenary of the competition. FIFA expanded the tournament this year from 32 to 48 teams, a move that delivered 40 additional matches for viewers. The governing body received criticism for its financial approach to the tournament, raising the cost of tickets, transport and hospitality in stadiums, as well as introducing a mid-game “hydration break”, which was widely viewed as a way to introduce more advertisements into broadcasts. Spain and Argentina at this year’s World Cup final at New York New Jersey Stadium in July. Getty Images

FIFA has since been in turmoil after a failed bid to sell off parts of the World Cup to private equity. A big part of that approach in 2026 was its partnership with online sports betting company Bet365. Palfreyman said the broadcaster heavily promoted its opt-out feature in the lead-up to the World Cup to allow viewers to switch off gambling advertising when watching on digital streaming platform SBS On Demand. “We’ve seen quite a significant take-up from audiences of the opt-out, specifically in relation to gambling. Actually, what we’ve also seen is a significant reduction in audience complaints, which is really pleasing and shows that we’re balancing that best-in-class consumer experience with the really strong ad experience,” she said.

SBS has recently been subject to attacks by One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, who says she plans to abolish the broadcaster if elected in 2028. title: $40,000 wiped off the value of the average house over winter
text:

Property values are falling in almost every suburb in the country, with $40,000 wiped from the median value of the nation’s homes through winter as high interest rates, the federal government’s budget tax changes and low levels of affordability crunch the entire market. Figures released by Cotality show the value of 93 per cent of all properties in capital city suburbs fell during winter, double the proportion that had gone backwards during autumn, creating an economic problem for the Reserve Bank and a political issue for the Albanese government. Across the nation’s capital cities, dwelling values dropped by 1.1 per cent in August to be down by 3.7 per cent over the past three months. The median value slipped to $990,394 compared to the $1.03 million recorded at the start of winter. Regional values are also falling, down by 0.4 per cent last month to be 1.2 per cent lower through the quarter.

Advertisement

The downturn is being driven by Sydney, where dwelling values dropped by 1.4 per cent in August to be down by a nation-leading 4.7 per cent through winter. The city’s median house value dropped by 1.8 per cent last month, taking it below $1.5 million for the first time in more than a year. Related Article Property prices In a slump: Warning house prices won’t rebound until 2028 Values fell in every capital city bar Darwin, easing by 1.1 per cent in Melbourne and Canberra, 1 per cent in Brisbane, 0.8 per cent in Adelaide and Perth and by 0.2 per cent in Hobart. Sydney and Melbourne values are down by 4.6 per cent and 4.7 per cent, respectively, from August last year. By contrast, values are still 15.6 per cent higher in Perth, by 14.6 per cent in Darwin and 10.8 per cent in Brisbane. The nation’s property slowdown accelerated after Treasurer Jim Chalmers revealed changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax concessions in the May budget.

Advertisement

The government has said its changes are aimed at improving housing affordability for young Australians. Despite the drop in values this year, every city bar Melbourne is still up on where it was five years ago while values in Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth are more than double their 2016 levels. But it has faced an increasingly strident political attack over the fallout from the tax changes, with the Coalition accusing the government of trying to “destroy” the wealth of Australians held in their homes. House values across the nation have fallen through winter. Joe Armao House values, particularly among the most expensive properties, are falling fastest and are down by 3.3 per cent so far this year. By contrast, the values of units and apartments have slipped by 1.8 per cent through 2026. Cotality research director Tim Lawless said values had now fallen for five consecutive months to sit 3.6 per cent below their peak in March.

Advertisement

He said demand across the entire market was falling while the number of homes up for sale was 24 per cent up on the same point last year. “What started as a more concentrated easing across higher-value segments has now become a much

more generalised softening, with the vast majority of capital city suburbs recording some level of decline,” he said. “The shift in selling conditions means buyers are generally facing less competition, while vendors are having to be more realistic on price as stock levels rise and days on market extend.” Property prices started to slow in February when the Reserve Bank delivered the first of three interest rate hikes so far this year. Markets believe the bank will push the cash rate to 4.6 per cent by November to deal with high inflation.

Advertisement

The University of Queensland underpaid about 16,400 professional and academic employees a total of $11 million. Jamila Toderas About 16,400 staff were shorted an average of $564 each, with the underpayments ranging from more than $41,600 – including interest and superannuation – to less than $1.

Mathieson jnr wrote to staff on Tuesday, claiming a joint investigation by The Sydney Morning Herald, The Age and The Australian Financial Review used “selective reporting” that lacked context. Star chief executive Bruce Mathieson jnr has defended his leadership of the casino. On Saturday, the investigation detailed serious concerns about Star’s compliance and problem gambling systems. Eight insiders, speaking on the condition of anonymity, alleged there had been an erosion of governance under Mathieson jnr’s leadership, while internal documents revealed Star repeatedly ignored warnings to fix a safety flaw on the rooftop deck of its Brisbane casino precinct before a young worker used it to scale a barrier and fall to her death. Mathieson jnr is the son of billionaire publican Bruce Mathieson snr and a former director at Endeavour, which owns the Dan Murphy’s bottle shop business and a string of pubs with poker machines. title: Ray-I? Ray Martin comes face to face with AI version of himself in SBS’ 2027 line-up

CultureTV & radioAustralian TV Ray-I? Ray Martin comes face to face with AI version of himself in SBS’ 2027 line-up Karl Quinn September 1, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ray Martin will come face to face with an AI-driven deep fake version of himself in a bid to understand the threats and opportunities posed by the rise of artificial intelligence in Ray Martin is Misinformed. The documentary is one of the highlights of the slate unveiled in SBS’ annual upfront presentation — a showcase of its most eye-catching (and ad-friendly) content of the year ahead — in Sydney on Tuesday. The broadcaster also announced that it has secured the rights to the 2030 FIFA World Cup, which will be staged in Spain, Portugal and Morocco. This follows the record-breaking ratings for this year’s tournament, which was watched, the network claims, by 8 million Australians. “For almost 50 years, SBS has been the spiritual home of the world game,” said managing director Jane Palfreyman. “Football has always reflected the Australia we are, and the Australia we aspire to be, a nation shaped by many cultures, communities, and stories. That’s why the FIFA World Cup on SBS matters. Because when SBS is doing its job well, Australia sees itself a little more clearly. I can’t think of a time when that has mattered more.” Joseph Maxwell, the network’s head of factual, said that in the Ray Martin-fronted documentary “we actually create Ray-I, an AI version of Ray, and by the end of the show you cannot tell who’s Ray and who’s Ray-I.”

Advertisement

Ray Martin will meet an AI version of himself. Will he know which is which? SBS “It’s pretty unsettling for Ray at certain moments. The model grows; it starts off not sounding like him and by the end, you feel you’re in the room with two Rays. It’s got his voice, it’s got his pauses. They say AI can’t have a sense of humour, but it certainly picks up some of his tone and playfulness by the end.” The show is not merely an exercise in what’s possible, Maxwell adds. It’s a meditation on what the fact that it is possible means — especially for the notion of truth in reporting. “Ray’s entire world has been journalism, and now journalism is under threat like it’s never been before. And Ray-I in some ways represents that threat. But in some ways it represents a solution, too.” Related Article Streaming This Emmy nominee is a star in America. At home in Australia, no one knows his name Maxwell highlighted a number of other notable documentaries in the slate, including Dan Goldberg’s Bondi, a “minute by minute” account of the events of December 14, 2025 from the perspective of those who were there.

Advertisement

“This has got no narration; it’s all told by the people who were there,” says Maxwell. “And it paints a broader portrait of antisemitism, a broader portrait of social cohesion, a broader portrait of multicultural Australia.” Similarly confronting is 2.6 Seconds, a four-part documentary series about the killing of Kumanjayi Walker by Northern Territory police officer Zachary Rolfe in 2019. Marking the directorial debut of Darren Dale, co-founder of production powerhouse Blackfella Films, the series has all the marks, Maxwell says, of being a “channel-defining” commission. “It’s a proper, landmark, premium true-crime show that reveals something really fascinating about Australia, doesn’t tell you what to think, but allows you to explore the evidence, explore the story,” he says. “And I think we will be holding this up as the kind of show that only SBS does – really distinctive, really bold and absolutely gripping.” Samuel Johnson presents Homeless 300, a new documentary series for SBS. Alone Australia will be back, and again the contestants will have to try to survive in the Arctic Circle. It will be in a different location to the season currently airing, and they’ll be going in later, so the harsh winter conditions will begin to bite earlier. But the biggest change will be that this time they’re allowed to hunt.

Advertisement

The Sami people’s sacred animals will not be on the menu, though. “There will be no reindeer harmed in the making of this show, I guarantee you that,” says Maxwell. “There are birds they can hunt, there are other animals they can hunt. But I can’t really reveal too much because the cast don’t know the details yet.” If Alone is all about people who opt to sleep rough in pursuit of a big cash prize, Homeless 300 will look at the plight of those who have no choice in the matter. Presented by Samuel Johnson, the show takes its name from the fact that 300 Australians are turned away from homeless shelters each night. And it’s a subject that resonates deeply with the Gold Logie-winning actor. “I don’t think I’ve ever seen a presenter so angered by the society in which we live,” says Maxwell. “He’s out there looking at this issue, and he’s just absolutely gobsmacked and asks us, ‘What as a nation can we do, and how did we get to this place?’”

The three-part series marks a return to the topic SBS explored with Filthy Rich and Homeless back in 2017, but from a fresh angle. “And the sad thing is that issue has not changed,” says Maxwell. “The show is very much looking at solutions as well as the problems.” If the SBS slate is rich in hard-hitting factual content – including a series in which Marc Fennell revisits the Hilton Bombing of 1978, and sits down with Evan Pederick, the man who confessed to the act, was jailed for it, but whose testimony was later deemed unreliable – it is noticeably thin on locally produced scripted content. The network announced just three commissions for its Digital Originals program, which has previously produced The Tailings and this year’s Logie-winning Homebodies. Ethan Hawke plays Lee Raybon, a self-styled “truthstorian”, in The Lowdown. The new series are adventure drama Mangrove Mansion, supernatural First Nations story Pretty Deadly and a social media comedy about feuding friends, Tantrum. But with a combined running time of just three hours, the slate does little to allay concerns about the parlous state of Australian drama and comedy on free-to-air television.

McLaren Minerals has tabled the best batch of high-grade heavy mineral (HM) assays to date from its flagship McLaren titanium project in the Eucla basin, Western Australia, with the latest drilling returning a length-weighted average of 5.44 per cent HM over an average thickness of 16.2m, all from surface. The impressive results come from a set of 74 holes covering 1199m of sampling and represent a solid step-up from the 4.96 per cent HM average unveiled in the previous crop of results. The drilling is part of a major program designed to increase confidence in the project’s existing 529-million-tonne resource. McLaren Minerals has received more high-grade assays from its titanium-rich project in the western Eucla Basin of Western Australia. The standout intercept was a hefty 21-metre section from surface grading 7.61 per cent HM. Other notable results included 18m at an even stronger 8.06 per cent HM from surface and another 18-metre hit from surface going 7.55 per cent HM. The company says the latest assay results continue to demonstrate a strong and consistent grade profile across the deposit. Without applying any HM cut-off, 66 of the 74 holes, or 89 per cent, averaged at least four per cent HM.

Advertisement

‘To return a length-weighted average of 5.44% HM over an average thickness of 16.2m is quite remarkable.’ McLaren Minerals managing director Simon Finnis Delving deeper into the numbers, 62 per cent of the holes averaged at least five per cent HM, and 24 holes, representing 32 per cent of the suite, came in at or above an impressive six per cent HM. The results also confirmed substantial mineralised thickness from surface, with 54 holes, or 73 per cent, returning at least 15m of completely sampled mineralisation. A further 11 holes hit at least 21m of mineralisation from surface. Higher-grade zones also appear to be a feature within the broader mineralised profile, with nearly a third of the holes hitting grades of at least 10 per cent HM over one metre. The peak one-metre result was a stellar 16.43 per cent HM from a shallow depth of 8m. McLaren Minerals managing director Simon Finnis said: “This is the strongest set of results yet from the 2026 drilling program. All from surface and across 1,199m of sampling, to return a length-weighted average of 5.44% HM over an average thickness of 16.2m is quite remarkable. The grade profile appears to be strengthening as we move south through the deposit, and what we’re seeing is consistently mineable grade and widths from surface across the entire dataset. Every batch seems to outdo the last.”

Advertisement

The news lands at a time when the broader mineral sands sector in Western Australia continues to be active, with major players such as Sheffield Resources recently restarting operations at its Thunderbird project, highlighting the industry’s ongoing viability. Titanium is now recognised by governments as a critical mineral essential for aerospace, defence and new energy technologies, making the development of large-scale domestic projects such as McLaren increasingly strategically important. Adding weight to the project, metal prices also appear supportive, with recent US Geological Survey data showing rutile holding firm at around US$1450 (A$2020) per tonne and ilmenite at US$350 (A$487) per tonne, providing a solid commercial backdrop for McLaren’s development plans. The McLaren project sits in the western Eucla basin and hosts a significant JORC-compliant resource of 529 million tonnes at 4.5 per cent HM, containing 23.7 million tonnes of in-situ heavy minerals. The inventory currently comprises 249 million tonnes in the indicated category and 280 million tonnes in the inferred category. The current drilling program is designed to upgrade a larger portion of the resource to the higher-confidence indicated category, which will then underpin a maiden ore reserve estimate and a bankable feasibility study. To date, McLaren has received 6671 assays from 11,568m drilled, which equates to 58 per cent of the total samples, suggesting plenty more newsflow is on its way.

With assays still rolling in and each batch seemingly outdoing the last, McLaren is systematically de-risking what is already a massive titanium deposit. As the company continues to build a more detailed picture of the grade and consistency across the project, it appears to be steadily marching towards a resource upgrade and the all-important feasibility studies that could transform it from an explorer into a developer. Jetstar has conducted its first test flight to Western Sydney International, ensuring that the plane’s taxi routes to the gates, the aerobridge, and the fuelling process all go as expected. Flight JQ7990 from Melbourne carried a crew but no passengers, and arrived 14 minutes early at 9.16am. The Jetstar A320 landed safely at Western Sydney International on Tuesday. Jetstar chief pilot captain Tyrone Simes said the “flight was about getting to know the airport before we carry customers,” particularly around ground service equipment. “It’s quite a collaborative team effort between the different departments on the ground, both in the flight deck cabin co-ordination and with refuelling procedures,” he said. The flight, designed as a test run of what will be regular operations, landed at a moment of heightened scrutiny about the safety of Australian aviation. Sydney Airport in the city’s east has seen a rash of incidents on the ground, which has raised questions about the staff and workload of the Sydney Airport Tower’s air traffic controllers. Western Sydney International uses a digital control tower, with flights into and out of the airport monitored by humans at a remote location in Eastern Creek, NSW. A pilot in the cockpit of Jetstar’s first flight into Western Sydney Airport. Sam Mooy

The airport handled bags of mock passengers as part of the trial flight. Sam Mooy Western Sydney Airport operates without a traditional manned air traffic control tower. Sam Mooy The Jetstar’s trial flight also let the Western Sydney Airport ground team practise their work with mock customers. Hundreds of volunteers acted as passengers to test the boarding and baggage systems, but did not actually participate in the flight. The Jetstar plane also conducted the test to ensure the flight crew’s ability to navigate around the taxiways and the infrastructure around the airport. Simes said the use of a Western Sydney’s digital air traffic control tower made no difference in the landing of the A320. “It was seamless actually,” Simes said.

Simes said he was confident that there will be enough air traffic controllers in Sydney to handle two airports when Western Sydney opens fully on October 25. “We’re working very closely with Airservices [Australia] on some of the issues that have been raised of late. “Of course we wouldn’t operate if the environment wasn’t safe,” said Simes. “So we’re absolutely confident that Airservices are able to satisfy those requirements.” “And we’ll continue to work on the issues that need [to be addressed],” he said. Larvotto Resources’ Hillgrove gold-antimony mine in New South Wales comes to life as ore feeds the ball mill. Larvotto shares have blasted from just 9.5 cents to a high of $1.67. Even at the current $1.14, the company boasts a thumping $587 million market capitalisation – a spectacular re-rating from a deal struck for relative pocket change. The project came with a sizeable inheritance, giving Larvotto a head start most mine developers could only dream of – underground workings, a processing plant, grid power and water systems, after previous operators sunk more than $150M into infrastructure. The company completed a prefeasibility study in August 2024 and a definitive feasibility study in May 2025, prior to funding, underground development, plant refurbishment, and staged commissioning. The first development ore from the underground Metz mining area reached surface stockpiles in May, three months ago, before crushing and screening were commissioned in July. Larvotto has also added the operational and technical expertise to capitalise on those foundations, growing its workforce beyond 180 people, with 95 per cent of Hillgrove’s operations crew based in NSW’s New England region.
