The 254-square-kilometre historic Hillgrove project, 23 kilometres east of Armidale, packs a hefty 1.7-million-ounce gold-equivalent resource across six key mining areas, with its antimony-gold riches locked up in a network of structurally controlled hydrothermal veins. Larvotto Resources managing director Ron Heeks said: “In less than three years, we have taken Hillgrove from acquisition, resource and reserve assessment, PFS, DFS, funding and construction to production, establishing Larvotto as Australia’s largest antimony producer and a globally significant new source of this essential critical mineral.” With the start-up in the rear view mirror, focus is now firmly on developing avenues to add future mine feed as Larvotto pursues a multi-decade operation centred on the existing processing hub. The company has resource growth opportunities around established mining areas such as Metz, as well as exploration targets elsewhere across the wider Hillgrove field. There is also scope to broaden the project’s production mix, with near-term plans to produce tungsten concentrate. Its tungsten occurs as scheelite within its broader mineralised vein systems and an already installed, though currently dormant, gravity circuit offers a potential pathway to add a third metal to the gold-antimony mix. Hillgrove is also intended to anchor a broader critical-minerals portfolio. Larvotto’s other assets include its Mt Isa copper, gold and cobalt project in Queensland and Eyre multi-metals and lithium project near Norseman in Western Australia, providing growth exposure beyond NSW.

However, it’s the company’s timing at Hillgrove that has the tongues wagging. New production is poised to ride a wave of booming antimony demand across renewable energy, electronics, artificial intelligence and defence as the West scrambles to secure alternative supply. The metal is one of three minerals prioritised alongside rare earths and gallium under Australia’s $1.2 billion Critical Mineral Reserve Strategy. China’s 2024 export restrictions have tightened the supply picture and Larvotto says no new ethically mined Western supply is expected in the near term. Hillgrove’s potential role in diversifying global antimony supply has been noticed. Larvotto is now part of the international push for reliable supply outside China-controlled sources, having recently engaged in high-level discussions with government and industry stakeholders in Australia, the US, Taiwan and Japan. From a fortuitous call to the administrators in October 2023 inquiring about the historic and dormant mine to a humming processing plant with first revenue on the horizon, Larvotto has successfully navigated the difficult transition from developer to producer. title: A beloved show vanished from the stage for almost half a century. It’s finally returning
text:
In a program that brings together the old and new, The Australian Ballet is digging into its archives and bringing back a long-missed favourite, with Frederick Ashton’s Cinderella returning to the stage after a 47-year absence.

“I wanted to bring back the works that made [their] mark in this company and had decades long of runs,” says artistic director David Hallberg. “Cinderella is one of the great classics of the balletic repertoire. The score is unbelievably rich. And choreographically, I think Ashton’s version is very true to the story.” Ashton’s style, Hallberg adds, is “very specific and very demanding for dancers”.

Another returning classic is Hallberg’s reimagining of Swan Lake, which premiered in 2023. Three years later, Hallberg says there will be some tweaks with set and costume design, and emphasises the importance of going back to familiar works, of not keeping them static.

Belle Urwin and Saranja Crowe as cygnets in Swan Lake. Simon Schluter

“The danger is that it becomes a museum piece, and that’s honestly my biggest fear with a work like Swan is that it just becomes something we roll out, something we perform for audiences that love ballet or maybe are seeing ballet for the first time, and then we call it a day ... Swan Lake needs to be assessed for today’s audiences,” he says.

“I think the most blatant kind of evolution of bringing Swan Lake into today’s time is that technique in ballet has evolved. The legs are higher. There are more pyrotechnics in technique, and I don’t say that as a negative. I say that as dancers are jumping higher, the jumps have refined, the turns have refined, and so therefore, the choreography remains as it was, but I think it’s being executed to a greater standard.”

One of the more recent works featured in the upcoming program is a return season of Kunstkamer, a modern, critically acclaimed non-narrative work with music that moves from Janis Joplin to Beethoven. In 2022, The Australian Ballet was the first company to perform it outside of the Netherlands, and ever since, Hallberg – who had a cameo role in that season, which he will not be reprising – has been asked when it will be returning.

title: 'It hurts': Lionel Messi announces international retirement after World Cup final defeat
text:
In brief Lionel Messi has announced his retirement from international football.

His domestic contract with Inter Miami continues until the end of the 2028 season.

Lionel Messi said on Tuesday he was retiring from international football after leading Argentina to a second successive World Cup final in July.

The 39-year-old forward, who won the World Cup in 2022 and dragged his nation to the final in the United States only to lose to Spain, said the decision had been painful.

"It was a decision that hurt and still hurts deep in my soul but I understand that it is the right time," Messi wrote on Instagram.

"I swear I always gave everything, not just in the last few years when we won everything but before that too, and I always fought and gave my all for this shirt," he added.

Messi led Argentina to World Cup glory four years ago by winning the final against France in a penalty shootout in Doha, but his side lost 1-0 to a superior Spain side in the 2026 final in East Rutherford, New Jersey.

Following the death of his father Jorge in August, Messi had said he had "serious doubts" about continuing to play football of any sort for "much longer".

"I don't know what I'll do without you, I don't know how to go on. I just played football, and now I have serious doubts about continuing to do so for much longer," he said then.

Messi's contract with Major League Soccer club Inter Miami runs until the end of the 2028 season.

The highlight of Messi's international career was winning the 2022 World Cup in Qatar. Source: Getty / Jean Catuffe

In this year's finals, Messi inspired Argentina to another final by scoring eight goals and provided two assists in the dramatic late comeback against England in the semi-finals.

But the dream of lifting the trophy again proved one match too far as the South Americans lost to Spain at MetLife Stadium (dubbed New York New Jersey Stadium for the duration of the World Cup).

Messi was pictured in tears after receiving his loser's medal. He said afterwards that the pain of defeat was "immense" and that it would "take a long time for this wound to heal".

'Thank you for everything'

In his statement on Tuesday, the eight-time Ballon d'Or winner said it was time for a new generation of Argentina players to take up the torch.

"I love, I loved, and I will always love being on the national team," he wrote. "I gave everything I had, I have nothing more to give, and besides, there are some very talented young players coming up behind me who deserve to be there."

Reacting to the news, FIFA president Gianni Infantino called Messi "one of the greatest players our sport has ever seen" and thanked him for "bringing so much joy to millions of football fans".

First called up in 2005 by Jose Nestor Pekerman as an 18-year-old, Messi would go on to play 207 times for Argentina and become the country's leading scorer, with 125 goals.

Messi also won two Copa Americas in 2021 and 2024 during his 21-year international career.

Yet, before the trophy-laden later years, Messi did not hold the place in Argentine hearts reserved for other national idols such as Diego Maradona or Pope Francis.

After moving to Catalonia at 13 to join Barcelona, Messi could have represented Spain but chose Argentina.

His long-time team-mate Angel Di Maria, also a 2022 world champion, on Monday paid homage to Messi for this choice and his impact on the national team.

"We will be forever grateful to you for being Argentinian and for having taken Argentina to the top of the world," Di Maria said.

"For having chosen to be Argentinian when you could have chosen something else. Thank you for everything."

For Ernesto Godoy, a 38-year-old teacher in Buenos Aires, Messi's retirement from international football marks "the end of an incredible career, a sportsman of a calibre rarely seen".

"There was Maradona, then a void, then Messi, and now we're going to experience that void (again), life without Messi, just as Argentina did without Maradona," he told the Agence France-Presse news agency, of the player who hangs up his shirt assured of his place in the Argentine pantheon.

title: AusPost boss reveals future of letter deliveries a‌mid stamp price warning
text:
IN BRIEF Australia Post says it will keep home delivery, ruling out community mailboxes for Australian suburbs and towns.

Letter deliveries could become less frequent as Australia Post adapts to falling volumes, Graham says.

Australia Post has warned the cost of sending a letter could eventually rise to $2, as the postal service grapples with a continuing collapse in mail volumes.

Chief executive Paul Graham told SBS News that Australia Post will need to make further changes to the way letters are delivered as fewer Australians use the service, but has ruled out any plans to follow overseas postal services that have moved away from traditional home delivery.

"We continue to see letter decline, 15 per cent last year and we're now seeing letter volumes that we haven't seen since the 1930s," Graham said.

The company has already reduced letter deliveries to every second day and increased the price of a standard stamp, but Graham said further price increases and efficiencies would be needed as letter volumes continued to fall, including potentially reducing delivery frequency even further.

Graham said the company is "in the fight of our lives", as it navigates structural change and fierce parcel competition squeezes margins.

Stamp prices could reach $2

Graham said Australia Post's current $1.85 lowest-cost stamp remained among the cheapest in comparable economies.

He said that the price of a stamp could eventually rise, but argued the increase would have a relatively small impact on individual households.

He estimated a further increase to $2 would add less than a dollar a year to the cost for a typical household.

The changes are being driven by the widening gap between the cost of maintaining a nationwide letter service and the number of letters being sent.

Australia Post delivered 1.42 billion letters last financial year, almost 15 per cent fewer than the previous year.

At the same time, its parcels and services business continued to grow, generating a record $8.01 billion in revenue.

No plans to follow in the footsteps of global services

Despite the pressure on its traditional letter business, Graham said there were no plans for Australia Post to follow postal services overseas by abandoning home delivery or shifting customers towards community mailboxes.

He pointed to the different nature of Australian cities, suburbs and regional communities as a reason.

"The nature of our suburbs and regional towns does not lend itself to that solution," he said.

Instead, Graham said Australia Post wanted to tailor its services to the needs of different communities.

He said the organisation remained "absolutely committed" to ensuring efforts to reduce costs did not come at the expense of people living in regional and remote Australia.

Australia Post currently operates more than 4,000 retail outlets across the country, with about 2,500 in regional and remote areas.

Letters still have a future, though it is changing

Graham acknowledged there was a risk Australia Post could eventually require taxpayer support as its letter business continued to decline.

But he said the organisation had a pathway towards financial sustainability, which would require support from government, stakeholders, customers and the broader community.

The company recorded a pre-tax profit of $31.8 million for the latest financial year, although that result was supported by returns from property sales.

Graham said further changes to the postal service would be necessary as Australians increasingly shift from letters to parcels and digital communication.

He urged Australians to continue using Australia Post and supporting its network of licensees across metropolitan, regional and remote communities.

"We'll continue to deliver letters until the last letter needs to be delivered."

title: Why China is censoring footage of the Nepal-Tibet disaster
text:
In brief Videos circulating globally of the Tibet-Nepal flood disaster cannot be found on Chinese social media platforms.

The disaster has cast a spotlight on the tight controls over information from Tibet.

A natural disaster may not seem inherently political. But in Tibet, even footage of a flood can be sensitive.

As videos circulated widely on social media and in news reports last week, showing a devastating torrent of mud, water and debris tearing through a border post between Tibet and Nepal, correspondents in Beijing began to point out a striking absence: in China, the footage was nowhere to be seen.

The apparent censorship highlights the extraordinary sensitivity surrounding Tibet, one of the most tightly controlled regions under Chinese control, and the long and highly contested history stretching back hundreds of years.

Tsering Yangzom, a member of the Tibetan community in Newcastle, NSW, told SBS News her uncle works in the flood-affected region of Tibet, but she's been unable to contact him since the disaster and appears to have been blocked.

She suspects he may be concerned their communications are being monitored, but she's also "really, really worried" about whether he was affected by the deadly floods.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Normally, she says they speak briefly and intermittently on the Chinese messaging app WeChat, sometimes using coded language to protect her uncle.

"If he says the weather is good, then we can talk a little bit more about the normal life," she said. "But if he says the weather is not good and rainy or something ... that means that I can't talk much."

Tsering Yangzom said she communicates with her Tibetan relative in code to keep him safe. Source: Supplied

Human Rights Watch's Australia director, Daniela Gavshon, told SBS News censorship and self-censorship are pervasive in Tibetan areas.

"These information controls make it even harder to get accurate information, for families to locate loved ones, or to develop a good understanding of the disaster, its scale, its impact, and the response."

A brief history of China and Tibet

Tibet, isolated both geographically and diplomatically, sits atop a vast area of mountains and plateaus and is often referred to as the "roof of the world".

For centuries, it has had a complicated relationship with China. Beijing maintains that Tibet has been part of China since ancient times, while Tibetans say it had long been independent with its own unique culture, religion and language.

In 1950, troops from China's newly established communist government invaded Tibet and defeated Tibetan forces, in a move the Chinese government described as part of the "peaceful liberation" of the region.

The following year, Tibetan representatives signed an agreement recognising Chinese sovereignty over Tibet, while promising the region autonomy. Tibetan leaders say they were forced into this agreement.

Tensions over Chinese rule grew in the following years, leading to an uprising in 1959 in the Tibetan capital, Lhasa. Thousands are believed to have died during China's suppression of the uprising, and Tibet's spiritual and then-political leader, the Dalai Lama, fled to India, where he has lived in exile ever since.

In 1965, China formally established the Tibet Autonomous Region, which continues to exist today, though its autonomy is highly disputed.

Human rights groups and the Tibetan government-in-exile continue to accuse Chinese authorities of seeking to erase Tibetan religious practice, language and cultural expression, exercising total political control over the region, repressing dissent and blocking the flow of information in and out of Tibet.

Access to the region is tightly controlled, making reporting from within Tibet extremely difficult.

The BBC's China correspondent, Laura Bicker, said she has often found it easier to contact sources in North Korea than in Lhasa.

Why censor a flood?

According to various international media organisations, videos filmed and uploaded by local residents showing the disaster have been censored on Chinese social media platforms.

On Chinese social media platform RedNote, SBS Chinese was unable to find the widely viewed CCTV footage showing the flash flooding engulfing the Rasuwagadhi border crossing between Tibet and Nepal.

Chinese state media has, however, shown vision of recovery efforts.

"For China, everything is inherently political when it comes to Tibet," Zoë Bedford, executive officer of the Australia Tibet Council, told SBS News.

Source: SBS News

"What they're afraid of is people hearing Tibetan voices. They're afraid of people understanding the extent of China's mega-development in Tibet and how much they have been interfering in the environment."

Feng Chongyi, associate professor in China Studies at the University of Technology Sydney, said many Tibetans and Nepalese people blame the Chinese government, which has funnelled billions into developments in the region in a bid to harness its vast hydropower potential and resources.

"The Chinese government, of course, do not want that kind of opinion or discussion to spread to the international community," he told SBS News.

SBS News has approached the Chinese embassy for comment.

The Tibetan Plateau region, sometimes called the world's "Third Pole", has the world's largest ice mass outside the Arctic and Antarctic.

The Himalayan region is particularly vulnerable to a warming climate, with destabilising glaciers increasing the risk of sudden and catastrophic floods like the ones last week that have killed hundreds of people and left thousands more unaccounted for.

The disaster was triggered by a glacier collapse, which Chinese authorities and international experts have linked to climate change.

Just three months before the disaster, officials from China and Nepal met to discuss strengthening cooperation to monitor floods, weather and glacier-related hazards.

But two Nepali officials told the Reuters news agency they didn't receive as much information as they wanted from China on glacier risks and water levels, heightening fears that insufficient data sharing could make it harder to anticipate and prepare for natural disasters.

On Saturday, the Chinese embassy in Nepal posted a statement on X responding to accusations on Nepali social media that it had failed to warn Nepal of the mudslide disaster.

It said China faced significant challenges in monitoring risks in the vast, remote Himalayan region and had always shared "important information with the Nepali side in a timely manner".

title: Should smart glasses blur your face by default? Australia's tech watchdog thinks so
text:
In brief The Australian eSafety Commissioner has recommended changes to how smart glasses operate.

Further new protections will overhaul Australia's privacy laws related to social media, AI and smart glasses.

People's faces should automatically be blurred when being filmed by smart glasses as part of greater privacy measures, the online safety watchdog has urged.

In advice to industry, the eSafety Commissioner has called for extra protections to be put in place for smart glasses, or glasses with cameras attached to them.

The growing uptake of the technology, prompted by cheap versions of the products being sold in outlets such as Kmart, has increased concerns about privacy and people being filmed without their consent.

The commissioner said faces of people being filmed should be blurred by default if they have not given consent, with clearer indicators being given for when the glasses are recording video.

"Companies selling smart glasses must balance the benefits of the technology with the need to protect users and the public," the commissioner said.

"As smart glasses become more common, they may create new ways to perpetrate harms."

The eSafety Commissioner said the rapid evolution of the technology meant there was still a chance for extra safety features to be baked into the products before harms became more widespread.

"They may become increasingly interconnected with and create new ways to perpetrate different types of harms, such as image-based abuse, adult cyber abuse, cyberbullying of children, or the livestreaming of violent or other harmful content," the advice said.

"The harms linked to covert recording are not hypothetical. They are real and already occurring."

Among the concerns listed by the commissioner was how the glasses could be used by "pick-up artists" who use the glasses to film women without their knowledge.

"Most of the women do not realise they are being filmed. These posts often attract misogynistic comments, compounding the harm," the commissioner said.

"Used in this way, smart glasses can reinforce and normalise watching, recording and controlling women in public without their knowledge."

The commissioner has also called for livestreaming from the glasses to operate on a delay, as well as for recording to be disabled when the glasses are not being worn.

Attorney-General Michelle Rowland wrote to the privacy commission earlier this month to investigate whether extra regulations for smart glasses were needed.

The Greens have called for a 12 month ban on the importation of smart glasses.

Under changes the minor party will bring to parliament, the filming, storing or sharing of footage from the glasses without consent would be a breach of privacy laws.

Social media and deletion requests

Rowland is also set to outline further changes to privacy laws, including the right to erasure, on Monday.

The policy would mean social media users can ask tech companies to delete their personal information published online or held by the platforms.

The draft laws will not apply to media organisations publishing news articles.

Rowland said the privacy laws were needed to keep up with technology changes.

"The right to erasure will help put more control in the hands of Australians, allowing personal information to be destroyed from large digital platforms," she said.

"We must ensure appropriate safeguards are placed around technology and stop the erosion of our privacy protections."

The federal government will also roll out extra protections for identity documents online.

A service called IDLock will allow people to block or unblock the use of identity documents such as passports.

IDLock will be made available through the government's MyGov platform from 2027 after a small-scale trial in late 2026.

"Australians deserve to have control over how their personal identity information, such as their driver licence or passport, is used to verify their identity online," Rowland said.

"As data breaches, scams and cyber-enabled crime continue to evolve, Australia's approach must evolve with them."

title: 'Massive changes': What you might find missing in Aussie supermarkets
text:
In Brief A social media trend known as "sardinemaxxing" has seen sardines cleared from supermarket shelves after hot demand.

Experts say the social media trend could be dangerous for other fish.

Walk down the canned fish aisle at your local supermarket right now, and there's a good chance you'll find a gap where the tinned sardines used to be, as a viral TikTok trend sends a wave of new fans in search of the small, oily fish.

The trend, dubbed "sardinemaxxing", has seen influencers push sardines as a beauty and wellness must-have, with some calling them "Botox on a fork" for their purported skin, hair, and anti-ageing benefits.

But experts say the trend raises real questions about where those sardines are coming from — and what happens if the hype spreads to other seafood.

Why groceries are going viral

Sardines are just the latest grocery item swept up in a social media-driven buying frenzy.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Cottage cheese and Greek yoghurt both had their moment in the past year, part of a broader "proteinmaxxing" wave prizing high-protein foods.

Lisa Asher, a retail and supermarket expert at the University of Sydney Business School, said the pattern is driven by a mix of influencer culture and wellness trends.

"What bothers me isn't that the kids are eating sardines … it's that they're taking advice now from people who are probably not people you should be listening to," Asher said.

"It's a new form of advertising with a lot of unknowns — we don't really know who's paying who and how much they're making out of it. That is a problem.

"In magazines, we used to look at celebrities, but celebrities have been replaced by influencers."

She said the trends all follow a similar pattern: demand increases, the product goes out of stock, prices sometimes rise, and eventually, when the hype cools down, it comes back in stock.

"But this is a product that is made from fish in the sea," she adds. "We don't want to overfish because suddenly, then we have none."

Canned sardines can be hard to come by these days thanks to a new social media trend. Source: Getty / Newscast / Universal Images Group

The big catch

That's where the environmental risks come in.

Adrian Meder, sustainable seafood program manager at the Australian Marine Conservation Society, says history shows a sudden cultural appetite for a particular seafood can do serious damage — pointing to shark fin soup, sea cucumber and some tuna fisheries as species pushed towards collapse by surging demand.

"We've yet to see online popularity as a driver of major declines in our oceans, but a cultural surge in popularity of a seafood has time and time again decimated populations of species from tunas, to sharks, to abalone, to sea cucumbers," Meder told SBS News.

"Online popularity is clearly capable of producing massive changes in consumer demand."

There's also a traceability problem: much of the tinned sardines on Australian shelves is imported, and it can be difficult to know where a can came from or how sustainably it was caught.

Jonathan Smart, an affiliate senior research scientist at James Cook University, agrees that origin matters.

He co-authored a study, released last week, that found Australia ranked just 52nd in seafood production, despite having about eight million square kilometres of fishing waters.

"The fisheries that a lot of our imported seafood comes from are actually quite unsustainable — and Australia imports a lot of seafood when perhaps it shouldn't," Smart told SBS News.

"By importing so much seafood, we're essentially exporting our environmental footprint to other countries that don't have the same level of management that we do."

He worries a viral trend like this one could make that problem worse.

"If a trend like this is popping up and all of a sudden you've got greater consumption of a species, the fear I would have is that then is going to lead to, again, a greater surge in that imported seafood.

"We just don't know if that's going to have the same sustainability levels as if you were actually consuming something locally."

A resilient little fish

But of all the species to go viral, sardines might be one of the best placed to handle their 15 minutes of fame.

Smart says sardines are a fast-growing, short-lived species with rapid turnover, making them naturally resilient to heavy fishing.

Because changes in biomass are driven more by environmental conditions — like ocean upwellings — rather than fishing activity, sardine and anchovy fisheries are some of the biggest in the world, he said.

"They can actually provide a really, really big harvest from them normally under sustainable conditions, depending on the fishery that they're coming from."

Locally, there's also a genuine opportunity: Australia's biggest fishery is a sardine fishery in South Australia — a fact Smart says is little known because much of the catch goes to aquaculture feed.

"Very little of it actually goes to human consumption," he said. "That's why I often recommend to people that we should be eating more sardines because that is a really sustainable fishery.

"We catch a lot of fish from it, and there's a lot of opportunity."

Meder agrees that there's room for Australians to put more sardines on their plate.

"Some cultures, including many Australian communities, actually used to eat a lot more sardines than they do now," he said, pointing to a shift in seafood consumption to more environmentally vulnerable, less abundant, and expensive fish species — of which trends like these could help reverse.

But that only holds if the sardines on the shelf are actually Australian — which means consumers may need to check labels and do a bit of Googling before putting them in their shopping basket.

So while sardines may be getting the limelight for just a brief period before scrollers move on to the next trend, if there's anything we can take from it, it's that the humble little sardine is actually built for this moment.

Viking Mines has struck high-grade tungsten from the first reconnaissance sampling program at its Long and Terrell projects in Nevada, USA, with assays returning grades of up to 2.7 per cent tungsten trioxide. Management says the results confirm rich mineralisation at two historic mine sites and underscore the potential for a significant tungsten endowment across the portfolio beyond its flagship Linka project. At the company’s Long project, continuous channel sampling across old-timer’s underground and surface workings delivered a solid 1.8-metre intersection grading 1.8 per cent tungsten trioxide, featuring a higher-grade 0.45m core running at an impressive 2.7 per cent. A second channel sample returned 1.35m at 0.6 per cent tungsten trioxide. Viking Mines Terrell tungsten project in Nevada, USA. In its day, the Long mine reportedly produced 17,000 tonnes at 0.6 per cent tungsten trioxide from two separate underground mines. The mineralisation is hosted in a skarn setting along an intrusive contact, a geological environment known for hosting significant tungsten deposits. Over at the Terrell project, which includes the historic Terrell underground mine, reconnaissance work also hit the mark. A float sample of contact skarn returned an impressive 2.4 per cent tungsten trioxide, while granite-hosted veins yielded up to 1.7 per cent tungsten trioxide. Samples from a historical stockpile also confirmed the presence of mineralisation, grading between 0.4 and 0.5 per cent tungsten trioxide.

‘This provides us with the opportunity to contribute additional sources of tungsten mineralisation in parallel with Linka.’ Viking Mines managing director and chief executive officer Julian Woodcock Viking Mines managing director and chief executive officer Julian Woodcock said: “The strength of these early reconnaissance sampling results at both Long and Terrell speaks to the quality of the ground we have secured in Nevada. Both projects have returned high-grade tungsten from historic workings that have seen no modern exploration activity. Our primary focus remains on Linka as our most advanced asset, however the opportunity for additional mineralisation at our other Projects is not to be overlooked.” The timing of the discovery could hardly be better. Viking’s work in Nevada taps directly into a major geopolitical and industrial theme: the West’s urgent need to secure domestic supply chains for critical minerals such as tungsten. With China dominating global supply, recent price surges for ammonium paratungstate (APT) have highlighted the vulnerability of Western industrial and defence sectors. The US Geological Survey has flagged the western part of Nevada as a key tungsten skarn province, making any new high-grade discovery there particularly noteworthy. While the new results are encouraging, the Linka project remains Viking’s primary focus. Linka was a historical producer, churning out 65,000 tonnes at a solid grade of 0.5 per cent tungsten trioxide up until 1956, when operations ceased due to a weak tungsten price rather than a lack of ore. The company recently received approval from the US Bureau of Land Management to collect a 907-tonne bulk sample from the project’s historical surface stockpiles.

The plan is to toll treat the bulk sample locally to produce concentrate samples for offtake assessment with APT refineries. The company believes this processing route might provide a potential low-capital, rapid-restart model that could be rolled out across its broader Nevada portfolio, with the Long and Terrell projects also potentially serving as future sources of mineralised feed. With high-grade tungsten now confirmed at multiple historic mines and a clear path to production testing at its flagship Linka project, Viking appears to be building a multi-pronged strategy in a tier-one jurisdiction. As the West scrambles to secure its own supply of critical minerals, Viking might be in the right place at the right time to help solve a pressing supply-side headache. SBS has secured the rights to broadcast the FIFA World Cup 2030 in a $30 million-plus bid to remain “the spiritual home of football” after this year’s blockbuster event. The public broadcaster’s boss Jane Palfreyman said she was thrilled to see the tournament stay on SBS after more than 18 million fans watched the recent World Cup on the network over June and July. SBS chief executive Jane Palfreyman has claimed the rights to the World Cup for the broadcaster. Ben Symons Palfreyman declined to comment on the price SBS has agreed to pay, though sources with knowledge of the deal said it is above the $30 million rumoured to have been paid for the 2026 tournament. She said the World Cup was an opportunity to celebrate Australia’s modern culture. “We saw with this World Cup, it really brings Australians together across cultures, languages, and communities. We know that most Australians support not just one team, but two or three, so it’s the Socceroos plus a second or third team, either based on their sporting prowess or cultural heritage,” Palfreyman said ahead of SBS’ annual content showcase to media buyers in Sydney on Tuesday.

Advertisement

The costs of sports rights continue to rise, even as advertising revenues flowing to free-to-air television broadcasters have fallen drastically over the past five years. Live sports and news are the two remaining categories guaranteed to deliver audiences to TV networks, as evidenced by this year’s Cup which was held across Canada, Mexico and the United States – more than 1 million Australians watched 64 of its 104 matches. This year’s edition was held in a favourable time zone for Australians, with the majority of matches kicking off during daylight hours, and the latter stage games at 5am. But the next edition will be jointly hosted by Spain, Portugal and Morocco, which are eight hours behind Australia’s Eastern Standard Time in winter. There will also be one match held in each of Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay to mark the centenary of the competition. FIFA expanded the tournament this year from 32 to 48 teams, a move that delivered 40 additional matches for viewers. The governing body received criticism for its financial approach to the tournament, raising the cost of tickets, transport and hospitality in stadiums, as well as introducing a mid-game “hydration break”, which was widely viewed as a way to introduce more advertisements into broadcasts. Spain and Argentina at this year’s World Cup final at New York New Jersey Stadium in July. Getty Images

FIFA has since been in turmoil after a failed bid to sell off parts of the World Cup to private equity. Related Article FIFA World Cup UEFA prepares criminal complaint against Gianni Infantino over World Cup sale Unlike the ABC, which airs very little live sport due to budgetary constraints limiting its ability to outbid commercial broadcasters, SBS can offset the cost of rights packages like the World Cup by selling ads. A big part of that approach in 2026 was its partnership with online sports betting company Bet365. Palfreyman said the broadcaster heavily promoted its opt-out feature in the lead-up to the World Cup to allow viewers to switch off gambling advertising when watching on digital streaming platform SBS On Demand. “We’ve seen quite a significant take-up from audiences of the opt-out, specifically in relation to gambling. Actually, what we’ve also seen is a significant reduction in audience complaints, which is really pleasing and shows that we’re balancing that best-in-class consumer experience with the really strong ad experience,” she said.

SBS has recently been subject to attacks by One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, who says she plans to abolish the broadcaster if elected in 2028. They want to participate in society. They feel like they belong. Helping people belong, whilst it’s really good for individuals, it’s good for communities, it’s good for democracy, and it’s good for Australia,” Palfreyman said. “Ultimately, that’s what we’re trying to do here at SBS.” SBS has also recommissioned Alone Australia for a fifth season, once again returning to the arctic circle after its most recent season took its cast of survivalists to Finland. title: $40,000 wiped off the value of the average house over winter
text:

PoliticsFederalProperty prices $40,000 wiped off the value of the average house over winter Shane Wright Updated September 1, 2026 — 2:26pm ,first published September 1, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Property values are falling in almost every suburb in the country, with $40,000 wiped from the median value of the nation’s homes through winter as high interest rates, the federal government’s budget tax changes and low levels of affordability crunch the entire market. Figures released by Cotality show the value of 93 per cent of all properties in capital city suburbs fell during winter, double the proportion that had gone backwards during autumn, creating an economic problem for the Reserve Bank and a political issue for the Albanese government. Across the nation’s capital cities, dwelling values dropped by 1.1 per cent in August to be down by 3.7 per cent over the past three months. The median value slipped to $990,394 compared to the $1.03 million recorded at the start of winter. Regional values are also falling, down by 0.4 per cent last month to be 1.2 per cent lower through the quarter.

Advertisement

The downturn is being driven by Sydney, where dwelling values dropped by 1.4 per cent in August to be down by a nation-leading 4.7 per cent through winter. The city’s median house value dropped by 1.8 per cent last month, taking it below $1.5 million for the first time in more than a year. Related Article Property prices In a slump: Warning house prices won’t rebound until 2028 Values fell in every capital city bar Darwin, easing by 1.1 per cent in Melbourne and Canberra, 1 per cent in Brisbane, 0.8 per cent in Adelaide and Perth and by 0.2 per cent in Hobart. Sydney and Melbourne values are down by 4.6 per cent and 4.7 per cent, respectively, from August last year. By contrast, values are still 15.6 per cent higher in Perth, by 14.6 per cent in Darwin and 10.8 per cent in Brisbane. The nation’s property slowdown accelerated after Treasurer Jim Chalmers revealed changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax concessions in the May budget.

Advertisement

The government has said its changes are aimed at improving housing affordability for young Australians. Despite the drop in values this year, every city bar Melbourne is still up on where it was five years ago while values in Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth are more than double their 2016 levels. But it has faced an increasingly strident political attack over the fallout from the tax changes, with the Coalition accusing the government of trying to “destroy” the wealth of Australians held in their homes. House values across the nation have fallen through winter. Joe Armao House values, particularly among the most expensive properties, are falling fastest and are down by 3.3 per cent so far this year. By contrast, the values of units and apartments have slipped by 1.8 per cent through 2026. Cotality research director Tim Lawless said values had now fallen for five consecutive months to sit 3.6 per cent below their peak in March.

Advertisement

He said demand across the entire market was falling while the number of homes up for sale was 24 per cent up on the same point last year. “What started as a more concentrated easing across higher-value segments has now become a much

more generalised softening, with the vast majority of capital city suburbs recording some level of decline,” he said. “The shift in selling conditions means buyers are generally facing less competition, while vendors are having to be more realistic on price as stock levels rise and days on market extend.” Property prices started to slow in February when the Reserve Bank delivered the first of three interest rate hikes so far this year. Markets believe the bank will push the cash rate to 4.6 per cent by November to deal with high inflation.

Advertisement

The bank’s efforts to curb inflation have been challenged by the fallout from the war against Iran, with oil prices pushing up above the $US90 a barrel on Monday. The International Energy Agency warned global oil supply was likely to be down 4.3 million barrels a day this year with current inventories being drawn down “at a rapid pace”. Figures released on Monday by the country’s prudential regulator showed growth in the value of investor mortgages held by the Commonwealth, Westpac, NAB and Westpac banks slowed through July in further confirmation that the budget changes have pushed many investors out of the property market. Cotality’s Tim Lawless says the spring real estate market is likely to be tough for those looking to sell. Janie Barrett Lawless noted that at the start of the slowdown in the market, values for low-priced homes – dominated by first home buyers – had held up. But even this sector was now in decline, with the situation not likely to improve through the spring selling season. “Premium markets are still generally recording weaker conditions, but lower-priced housing is becoming less insulated as affordability pressures and softer demand weigh more evenly across the market,” he said.

University of Queensland staff are preparing to stop work for half a day next week in their fight over pay and entitlements, as their employer signed an agreement to pay back thousands of employees it had shortchanged. The university signed an agreement with the Fair Work Ombudsman on Tuesday, a week before staff planned to stop work following stalled enterprise bargaining wage negotiations. The latest figures show the number of UQ employees underpaid through systemic faults has grown by more than 6000 people. The University of Queensland underpaid about 16,400 professional and academic employees a total of $11 million. Jamila Toderas About 16,400 staff were shorted an average of $564 each, with the underpayments ranging from more than $41,600 – including interest and superannuation – to less than $1.

Most of those who missed wages were casual employees, which National Tertiary Education Union UQ branch president Professor Andrew Bonnell said made up just under half the university’s workforce. Related Article University Queensland university shortchanges staff $1.3m in wages “It’s been a systemic problem that the higher education sectors relied too much on cheap, casual labour,” he said. “There’s still an awful lot of teaching being done by casuals and … we’ve also had people with PhDs who’ve been teaching the same course for many years, and they’re the group who really should have been converted [to a permanent position] by now.” Bonnell said the union was pushing to increase casual employees’ entitlements, which included raising superannuation rates to be equal to other staff members.

Advertisement

The union was also arguing for a larger pay increase than the 2.8 per cent offered by the university. Related Article University Queensland university finalises nearly $2m to underpaid staff “The university’s got about a half-billion-dollar surplus in the last two years … so we think UQ can do better than 2.8 per cent a year, which is below inflation,” Bonnell said. The underpayments came from system errors that ignored conditions laid out in enterprise agreements from 2014, 2018, and 2021. UQ Vice-Chancellor Deborah Terry said the errors related to base pay rates for casual academic staff with PhDs, missing overtime, and missing minimum engagement times, which lay out the minimum number of hours an employee can be paid after showing up for a shift.

“I would like to sincerely apologise again to current and former staff,” Terry said. “The university is implementing a range of measures – including improved systems and processes, compulsory training, enhanced assurance checks, and an independent audit – to ensure this does not happen in future.” University of Queensland Vice-Chancellor Professor Deborah Terry AO. Dan Peled The university first reported the issues to the ombudsman in early 2024 after uncovering them in a review that began in 2021. At the time, 9743 staff were owed backpay for errors spanning from 2023 back to 2017.

The university vowed to address the issues in early 2024. But on Tuesday, the Fair Work Ombudsman said some staff working at St Lucia, Herston, Dutton Park and Gatton continued to receive incorrect pay until this year. The university had repaid more than $9.6 million to current and former employees by Tuesday. It also paid a penalty of $175,000 to the ombudsman. Including interest, superannuation and the extra underpayments discovered since the review, the university will pay about $11 million. title: Star boss blames previous management for casino giant’s woes

Star Entertainment chief executive Bruce Mathieson jnr has blamed previous management for the struggling casino giant’s compliance problems, promising he will deliver a clean slate and cultural overhaul for the “long-suffering business”. Mathieson jnr wrote to staff on Tuesday, claiming a joint investigation by The Sydney Morning Herald, The Age and The Australian Financial Review used “selective reporting” that lacked context. Star chief executive Bruce Mathieson jnr has defended his leadership of the casino. Oscar Colman “The simple fact is that so little that had transpired in the past – including the immediate past before we took over less than nine months ago – was at a standard our regulators, governments, customers and communities should expect,” Mathieson jnr wrote in the email seen by the Herald and The Age. “We are working to change that. This will involve trying new things, recognising when they do not work, and making changes as required.”

Advertisement

On Saturday, the investigation detailed serious concerns about Star’s compliance and problem gambling systems. Eight insiders, speaking on the condition of anonymity, alleged there had been an erosion of governance under Mathieson jnr’s leadership, while internal documents revealed Star repeatedly ignored warnings to fix a safety flaw on the rooftop deck of its Brisbane casino precinct before a young worker used it to scale a barrier and fall to her death. Mathieson jnr is the son of billionaire publican Bruce Mathieson snr and a former director at Endeavour, which owns the Dan Murphy’s bottle shop business and a string of pubs with poker machines. The younger Mathieson took over as chief executive of Star following the completion of a $300 million rescue package with American casino giant Bally’s. The deal lifted his family’s stake in the business to 23 per cent, while Bally’s owns 37.7 per cent. Mathieson jnr wrote that he brought a “clean slate” to Star as well as a willingness to “listen and learn”. “There is no reason why cities as significant as Sydney, Brisbane and Gold Coast cannot have internationally recognised integrated resorts that add to the rich vibrancy of those cities,” he said. “Across the three properties the work that has been done to review the effectiveness and efficiency of the Star’s financial crime and safer gambling processes and practices … is ongoing and evolving. It’s disappointing to see such selective reporting of our confidential corporate information, without context.”

Advertisement

When 60 Minutes, The Age and the Herald first exposed allegations of Star’s governance failings in 2021, the then-executives at the casino firm sought to downplay the reporting, only for regulators to confirm the reports and strip the casino of its licence in late 2022. Since then, Star has struggled to make money from its casinos. Related Article Earnings season Star bleeds $307 million as auditors raise further doubts about its survival Major inquiries in 2022 and 2024 ultimately led to repeated cleanouts of management, as well as new state casino regulations that limit cash spending and require detailed checks on customers. Star is also facing a multimillion-dollar fine from AUSTRAC, the financial crimes watchdog, for historical misconduct.



In Sydney, Star’s licence is suspended. It has been overseen for almost four years by independent administrator Nick Weeks. Its licences to operate the Gold Coast and Brisbane casinos are not suspended but are also under Weeks’ oversight. A decision on whether Star can operate its own licences is due in September. NSW casino regulator Philip Crawford said on Monday he had ordered a fresh inquiry into Star following the investigation by the Herald and The Age. He is still deciding whether to hand Star back its licence to run its Sydney casino. A spokesman for the Office of Liquor and Gaming Regulation said the regulator had sought “urgent advice” from Weeks following the latest revelations. title: Ray-I? Ray Martin comes face to face with AI version of himself in SBS’ 2027 line-up
text:

CultureTV & radioAustralian TV Ray-I? Ray Martin comes face to face with AI version of himself in SBS’ 2027 line-up Karl Quinn September 1, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ray Martin will come face to face with an AI-driven deep fake version of himself in a bid to understand the threats and opportunities posed by the rise of artificial intelligence in Ray Martin is Misinformed. The documentary is one of the highlights of the slate unveiled in SBS’ annual upfront presentation — a showcase of its most eye-catching (and ad-friendly) content of the year ahead — in Sydney on Tuesday. The broadcaster also announced that it has secured the rights to the 2030 FIFA World Cup, which will be staged in Spain, Portugal and Morocco. This follows the record-breaking ratings for this year’s tournament, which was watched, the network claims, by 8 million Australians. “For almost 50 years, SBS has been the spiritual home of the world game,” said managing director Jane Palfreyman. “Football has always reflected the Australia we are, and the Australia we aspire to be, a nation shaped by many cultures, communities, and stories. That’s why the FIFA World Cup on SBS matters. Because when SBS is doing its job well, Australia sees itself a little more clearly. I can’t think of a time when that has mattered more.” Joseph Maxwell, the network’s head of factual, said that in the Ray Martin-fronted documentary “we actually create Ray-I, an AI version of Ray, and by the end of the show you cannot tell who’s Ray and who’s Ray-I.”

Advertisement

Ray Martin will meet an AI version of himself. Will he know which is which? SBS “It’s pretty unsettling for Ray at certain moments. The model grows; it starts off not sounding like him and by the end, you feel you’re in the room with two Rays. It’s got his voice, it’s got his pauses. They say AI can’t have a sense of humour, but it certainly picks up some of his tone and playfulness by the end.” The show is not merely an exercise in what’s possible, Maxwell adds. It’s a meditation on what the fact that it is possible means — especially for the notion of truth in reporting. “Ray’s entire world has been journalism, and now journalism is under threat like it’s never been before. And Ray-I in some ways represents that threat. But in some ways it represents a solution, too.” Related Article Streaming This Emmy nominee is a star in America. At home in Australia, no one knows his name Maxwell highlighted a number of other notable documentaries in the slate, including Dan Goldberg’s Bondi, a “minute by minute” account of the events of December 14, 2025 from the perspective of those who were there.

Advertisement

“This has got no narration; it’s all told by the people who were there,” says Maxwell. “And it paints a broader portrait of antisemitism, a broader portrait of social cohesion, a broader portrait of multicultural Australia.” Similarly confronting is 2.6 Seconds, a four-part documentary series about the killing of Kumanjayi Walker by Northern Territory police officer Zachary Rolfe in 2019. Marking the directorial debut of Darren Dale, co-founder of production powerhouse Blackfella Films, the series has all the marks, Maxwell says, of being a “channel-defining” commission. “It’s a proper, landmark, premium true-crime show that reveals something really fascinating about Australia, doesn’t tell you what to think, but allows you to explore the evidence, explore the story,” he says. “And I think we will be holding this up as the kind of show that only SBS does – really distinctive, really bold and absolutely gripping.” Samuel Johnson presents Homeless 300, a new documentary series for SBS. Alone Australia will be back, and again the contestants will have to try to survive in the Arctic Circle. It will be in a different location to the season currently airing, and they’ll be going in later, so the harsh winter conditions will begin to bite earlier. But the biggest change will be that this time they’re allowed to hunt.

Advertisement

The Sami people’s sacred animals will not be on the menu, though. “There will be no reindeer harmed in the making of this show, I guarantee you that,” says Maxwell. “There are birds they can hunt, there are other animals they can hunt. But I can’t really reveal too much because the cast don’t know the details yet.” If Alone is all about people who opt to sleep rough in pursuit of a big cash prize, Homeless 300 will look at the plight of those who have no choice in the matter. Presented by Samuel Johnson, the show takes its name from the fact that 300 Australians are turned away from homeless shelters each night. And it’s a subject that resonates deeply with the Gold Logie-winning actor. “I don’t think I’ve ever seen a presenter so angered by the society in which we live,” says Maxwell. “He’s out there looking at this issue, and he’s just absolutely gobsmacked and asks us, ‘What as a nation can we do, and how did we get to this place?’”

Advertisement

The three-part series marks a return to the topic SBS explored with Filthy Rich and Homeless back in 2017, but from a fresh angle. “And the sad thing is that issue has not changed,” says Maxwell. “The show is very much looking at solutions as well as the problems.” If the SBS slate is rich in hard-hitting factual content – including a series in which Marc Fennell revisits the Hilton Bombing of 1978, and sits down with Evan Pederick, the man who confessed to the act, was jailed for it, but whose testimony was later deemed unreliable – it is noticeably thin on locally produced scripted content. The network announced just three commissions for its Digital Originals program, which has previously produced The Tailings and this year’s Logie-winning Homebodies. McLaren Minerals has tabled the best batch of high-grade heavy mineral (HM) assays to date from its flagship McLaren titanium project in the Eucla basin, Western Australia, with the latest drilling returning a length-weighted average of 5.44 per cent HM over an average thickness of 16.2m, all from surface. The impressive results come from a set of 74 holes covering 1199m of sampling and represent a solid step-up from the 4.96 per cent HM average unveiled in the previous crop of results. The drilling is part of a major program designed to increase confidence in the project’s existing 529-million-tonne resource. McLaren Minerals has received more high-grade assays from its titanium-rich project in the western Eucla Basin of Western Australia. The standout intercept was a hefty 21-metre section from surface grading 7.61 per cent HM. Other notable results included 18m at an even stronger 8.06 per cent HM from surface and another 18-metre hit from surface going 7.55 per cent HM. The company says the latest assay results continue to demonstrate a strong and consistent grade profile across the deposit. Without applying any HM cut-off, 66 of the 74 holes, or 89 per cent, averaged at least four per cent HM.

Advertisement

‘To return a length-weighted average of 5.44% HM over an average thickness of 16.2m is quite remarkable.’ McLaren Minerals managing director Simon Finnis Delving deeper into the numbers, 62 per cent of the holes averaged at least five per cent HM, and 24 holes, representing 32 per cent of the suite, came in at or above an impressive six per cent HM. The results also confirmed substantial mineralised thickness from surface, with 54 holes, or 73 per cent, returning at least 15m of completely sampled mineralisation. A further 11 holes hit at least 21m of mineralisation from surface. Higher-grade zones also appear to be a feature within the broader mineralised profile, with nearly a third of the holes hitting grades of at least 10 per cent HM over one metre. The peak one-metre result was a stellar 16.43 per cent HM from a shallow depth of 8m. McLaren Minerals managing director Simon Finnis said: “This is the strongest set of results yet from the 2026 drilling program. All from surface and across 1,199m of sampling, to return a length-weighted average of 5.44% HM over an average thickness of 16.2m is quite remarkable. The grade profile appears to be strengthening as we move south through the deposit, and what we’re seeing is consistently mineable grade and widths from surface across the entire dataset. Every batch seems to outdo the last.”

Advertisement

The news lands at a time when the broader mineral sands sector in Western Australia continues to be active, with major players such as Sheffield Resources recently restarting operations at its Thunderbird project, highlighting the industry’s ongoing viability. Titanium is now recognised by governments as a critical mineral essential for aerospace, defence and new energy technologies, making the development of large-scale domestic projects such as McLaren increasingly strategically important. Adding weight to the project, metal prices also appear supportive, with recent US Geological Survey data showing rutile holding firm at around US$1450 (A$2020) per tonne and ilmenite at US$350 (A$487) per tonne, providing a solid commercial backdrop for McLaren’s development plans. The McLaren project sits in the western Eucla basin and hosts a significant JORC-compliant resource of 529 million tonnes at 4.5 per cent HM, containing 23.7 million tonnes of in-situ heavy minerals. The inventory currently comprises 249 million tonnes in the indicated category and 280 million tonnes in the inferred category. The current drilling program is designed to upgrade a larger portion of the resource to the higher-confidence indicated category, which will then underpin a maiden ore reserve estimate and a bankable feasibility study. To date, McLaren has received 6671 assays from 11,568m drilled, which equates to 58 per cent of the total samples, suggesting plenty more newsflow is on its way.

With assays still rolling in and each batch seemingly outdoing the last, McLaren is systematically de-risking what is already a massive titanium deposit. As the company continues to build a more detailed picture of the grade and consistency across the project, it appears to be steadily marching towards a resource upgrade and the all-important feasibility studies that could transform it from an explorer into a developer. title: Jetstar’s first flight to Western Sydney Airport arrives early

Jetstar has conducted its first test flight to Western Sydney International, ensuring that the plane’s taxi routes to the gates, the aerobridge, and the fuelling process all go as expected. Flight JQ7990 from Melbourne carried a crew but no passengers, and arrived 14 minutes early at 9.16am. The Jetstar A320 landed safely at Western Sydney International on Tuesday. Sam Mooy Pilot Tyrone Simes (left) with co-pilot Nick Copland, WSI chief operating officer Matt Duffy are after the arrival of the flight. Sam Mooy Members of the public have volunteered to act as passengers at a trial of Western Sydney International. Sam Mooy

Advertisement

Jetstar chief pilot captain Tyrone Simes said the “flight was about getting to know the airport before we carry customers,” particularly around ground service equipment. “It’s quite a collaborative team effort between the different departments on the ground, both in the flight deck cabin co-ordination and with refuelling procedures,” he said. The flight, designed as a test run of what will be regular operations, landed at a moment of heightened scrutiny about the safety of Australian aviation. Sydney Airport in the city’s east has seen a rash of incidents on the ground, which has raised questions about the staff and workload of the Sydney Airport Tower’s air traffic controllers. Western Sydney International uses a digital control tower, with flights into and out of the airport monitored by humans at a remote location in Eastern Creek, NSW. A pilot in the cockpit of Jetstar’s first flight into Western Sydney Airport. Sam Mooy

Advertisement

The airport handled bags of mock passengers as part of the trial flight. Sam Mooy Western Sydney Airport operates without a traditional manned air traffic control tower. Sam Mooy The Jetstar’s trial flight also let the Western Sydney Airport ground team practise their work with mock customers. Hundreds of volunteers acted as passengers to test the boarding and baggage systems, but did not actually participate in the flight. The Jetstar plane also conducted the test to ensure the flight crew’s ability to navigate around the taxiways and the infrastructure around the airport. Simes said the use of a Western Sydney’s digital air traffic control tower made no difference in the landing of the A320. “It was seamless actually,” Simes said.

Advertisement

Simes said he was confident that there will be enough air traffic controllers in Sydney to handle two airports when Western Sydney opens fully on October 25. “We’re working very closely with Airservices [Australia] on some of the issues that have been raised of late. “Of course we wouldn’t operate if the environment wasn’t safe,” said Simes. “So we’re absolutely confident that Airservices are able to satisfy those requirements.” “And we’ll continue to work on the issues that need [to be addressed],” he said. Western Sydney International’s chief operating officer Matt Duffy said that there have been 77 trials since they began last October, or roughly two a week, every week.

Advertisement

“We built the asset, then we wrap people process around that asset ... As we work through the trials, we learn more about the asset, then we take those learnings and put them back into our processes” Duffy said. Related Article Exclusive

Aviation VietJet to offer international flights from Western Sydney Airlines and planners are questioning how Western Sydney International will function alongside Sydney airport, which has capacity issues and its own ambitious plans for long-term growth through its recently released master plan for the next two decades. Duffy said trials were on track ahead of the launch of passenger flights. “Today’s trial flight represents an important part of our ongoing operational readiness program, which is all about preparing our staff, systems and processes to be as match-fit as possible when the airport opens for passengers next month,” he said.

Starting on October 25, Jetstar will operate up to 14 flights a week between Western Sydney and Melbourne, as well as daily flights to the Gold Coast, which had to be bumped up from four a week to meet demand. Jetstar will also fly three flights a week to Brisbane. It joins Qantas, Air New Zealand and Singapore Airlines as carriers committed to launch at the curfew-free airport. Vietnamese low-cost carrier VietJet has also signalled an interest in flying from Western Sydney to Vietnam from January. Later in 2027, VietJet expects to flying between Western Sydney and Thailand. title: NSW Hillgrove roars to life as Larvotto joins antimony producer ranks

Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears NSW Hillgrove roars to life as Larvotto joins antimony producer ranks Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Penny Taylor September 1, 2026 — 1:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. In a lightning-fast transformation, Larvotto Resources has crossed the development finish line and joined the producer ranks, firing up gold and antimony production at its 100 per cent-owned Hillgrove mine in New South Wales. The milestone anoints the company as Australia’s second – and by far its largest – antimony producer, with Hillgrove expected to supply seven per cent of global demand and more than half of supply outside China-controlled sources. Larvotto Resources’ Hillgrove gold-antimony mine in New South Wales comes to life as ore feeds the ball mill. With the processing plant now fully up and running, the operation is forecast to produce 4900 tonnes of antimony and 40,500 ounces of gold annually over an initial eight-year mine life. Adding to its credentials, routes to market are already established, with a seven-year Glencore gold concentrate offtake expected to cover 15,000 dry metric tonnes annually, alongside an antimony concentrate arrangement with Wogen Resources. The story behind Larvotto’s remarkable rise is almost as compelling as the mine itself. It was only in mid-2023 that management first knocked on the administrators’ door for the dormant Hillgrove operation. With no rival bidders stepping up to the plate, the company swooped with an opportunistic $8 million offer – including a $5 million environmental bond – and walked away with what would prove to be a brownfields bargain.

Advertisement

‘Becoming Australia’s biggest antimony producer is a significant achievement, particularly when securing reliable supply of antimony, has become a strategic priority for governments around the world.’ Larvotto Resources managing director Ron Heeks Less than three years later, the mothballed operation has been transformed into a producing gold-antimony mine and the market has come along for the ride. Larvotto shares have blasted from just 9.5 cents to a high of $1.67. Even at the current $1.14, the company boasts a thumping $587 million market capitalisation – a spectacular re-rating from a deal struck for relative pocket change. The project came with a sizeable inheritance, giving Larvotto a head start most mine developers could only dream of – underground workings, a processing plant, grid power and water systems, after previous operators sunk more than $150M into infrastructure. The company completed a prefeasibility study in August 2024 and a definitive feasibility study in May 2025, prior to funding, underground development, plant refurbishment, and staged commissioning. The first development ore from the underground Metz mining area reached surface stockpiles in May, three months ago, before crushing and screening were commissioned in July. Larvotto has also added the operational and technical expertise to capitalise on those foundations, growing its workforce beyond 180 people, with 95 per cent of Hillgrove’s operations crew based in NSW’s New England region.

Advertisement

The 254-square-kilometre historic Hillgrove project, 23 kilometres east of Armidale, packs a hefty 1.7-million-ounce gold-equivalent resource across six key mining areas, with its antimony-gold riches locked up in a network of structurally controlled hydrothermal veins. Larvotto Resources managing director Ron Heeks said: “In less than three years, we have taken Hillgrove from acquisition, resource and reserve assessment, PFS, DFS, funding and construction to production, establishing Larvotto as Australia’s largest antimony producer and a globally significant new source of this essential critical mineral.” With the start-up in the rear view mirror, focus is now firmly on developing avenues to add future mine feed as Larvotto pursues a multi-decade operation centred on the existing processing hub. The company has resource growth opportunities around established mining areas such as Metz, as well as exploration targets elsewhere across the wider Hillgrove field. There is also scope to broaden the project’s production mix, with near-term plans to produce tungsten concentrate. Its tungsten occurs as scheelite within its broader mineralised vein systems and an already installed, though currently dormant, gravity circuit offers a potential pathway to add a third metal to the gold-antimony mix. Hillgrove is also intended to anchor a broader critical-minerals portfolio. Larvotto’s other assets include its Mt Isa copper, gold and cobalt project in Queensland and Eyre multi-metals and lithium project near Norseman in Western Australia, providing growth exposure beyond NSW.

Advertisement

However, it’s the company’s timing at Hillgrove that has the tongues wagging. New production is poised to ride a wave of booming antimony demand across renewable energy, electronics, artificial intelligence and defence as the West scrambles to secure alternative supply. The metal is one of three minerals prioritised alongside rare earths and gallium under Australia’s $1.2 billion Critical Mineral Reserve Strategy. China’s 2024 export restrictions have tightened the supply picture and Larvotto says no new ethically mined Western supply is expected in the near term. Hillgrove’s potential role in diversifying global antimony supply has been noticed. Larvotto is now part of the international push for reliable supply outside China-controlled sources, having recently engaged in high-level discussions with government and industry stakeholders in Australia, the US, Taiwan and Japan. From a fortuitous call to the administrators in October 2023 inquiring about the historic and dormant mine to a humming processing plant with first revenue on the horizon, Larvotto has successfully navigated the difficult transition from developer to producer. The job now is to ramp output, bolt on tungsten and turn an initial eight-year mine into a multi-decade operation with Hillgrove firmly planted on the global critical-minerals stage. title: A beloved show vanished from the stage for almost half a century. It’s finally returning
text:
In a program that brings together the old and new, The Australian Ballet is digging into its archives and bringing back a long-missed favourite, with Frederick Ashton’s Cinderella returning to the stage after a 47-year absence.

“I wanted to bring back the works that made [their] mark in this company and had decades long of runs,” says artistic director David Hallberg. “Cinderella is one of the great classics of the balletic repertoire. The score is unbelievably rich. And choreographically, I think Ashton’s version is very true to the story.” Ashton’s style, Hallberg adds, is “very specific and very demanding for dancers”.

Another returning classic is Hallberg’s reimagining of Swan Lake, which premiered in 2023. Three years later, Hallberg says there will be some tweaks with set and costume design, and emphasises the importance of going back to familiar works, of not keeping them static.

Belle Urwin and Saranja Crowe as cygnets in Swan Lake. Simon Schluter

“The danger is that it becomes a museum piece, and that’s honestly my biggest fear with a work like Swan is that it just becomes something we roll out, something we perform for audiences that love ballet or maybe are seeing ballet for the first time, and then we call it a day ... Swan Lake needs to be assessed for today’s audiences,” he says.

“I think the most blatant kind of evolution of bringing Swan Lake into today’s time is that technique in ballet has evolved. The legs are higher. There are more pyrotechnics in technique, and I don’t say that as a negative. I say that as dancers are jumping higher, the jumps have refined, the turns have refined, and so therefore, the choreography remains as it was, but I think it’s being executed to a greater standard.”

One of the more recent works featured in the upcoming program is a return season of Kunstkamer, a modern, critically acclaimed non-narrative work with music that moves from Janis Joplin to Beethoven. In 2022, The Australian Ballet was the first company to perform it outside of the Netherlands, and ever since, Hallberg – who had a cameo role in that season, which he will not be reprising – has been asked when it will be returning.
